questions.question: Three parallel lines are cut by a transversal. The transversal creates segments of 8 between the first and second parallel lines, and 12 between the second and third parallel lines. A second transversal cuts the same three parallel lines, creating a segment of 10 between the first and second parallel lines. What is the length of the segment between the second and third parallel lines on the second transversal?
questions.explanation: By the Intercept Theorem, corresponding segments on two transversals cut by parallel lines are proportional: 8/12 = 10/x → x = (12 × 10)/8 = 120/8 = 15.
questions.trap: Students assume the second transversal also has a 12-unit segment (since 12 appears in the first transversal) or add/subtract rather than using proportionality.

questions.question:
In triangle PQR, line ST is parallel to QR with S on PQ and T on PR. PS = 4, SQ = 6.
Quantity A: The ratio ST/QR
Quantity B: 2/5
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: By the Triangle Proportionality Theorem, ST/QR = PS/PQ. PQ = PS + SQ = 4 + 6 = 10. So ST/QR = 4/10 = 2/5. Quantity A = Quantity B.
questions.trap: Students compute PS/SQ = 4/6 = 2/3 as the ratio, using the part-to-part ratio instead of the part-to-whole ratio PS/PQ.

questions.question: Lines r and s are parallel. Transversal t makes an angle of α with line r, and transversal u makes an angle of β with line r, each measured above the line and to the right of the transversal. Which of the following correctly describes the angles that t and u make with line s, measured in the same position (above s and to the right of the transversal)?
options: A. Both angles equal 180° − α and 180° − β respectively
B. The angles equal α and β respectively
C. The angles equal β and α (swapped)
E. The angles equal α and β only if t and u are parallel to each other
questions.explanation: When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, corresponding angles are equal. Transversal t makes angle α with r, so in the corresponding position it makes angle α with s. Independently, transversal u makes angle β with r and therefore β with s. Each transversal is treated on its own; the presence of a second transversal changes nothing.
questions.trap: Choice A applies the co-interior (same-side interior) rule and subtracts from 180°, although the angles described are in corresponding, not co-interior, positions. Choice C assumes two transversals exchange their angles. Choice D averages the two angles, as if the transversals interacted. Choice E adds a condition that is never needed: corresponding angles are equal because r and s are parallel, whatever the relationship between t and u.

questions.question: Lines a and b are parallel, cut by transversal t. Angle 1 is an acute angle at line a that lies between the two lines. Select ALL statements that are true.
options: A. The corresponding angle at line b equals Angle 1
B. The co-interior angle at line b equals Angle 1
C. The alternate interior angle at line b equals Angle 1
D. The co-interior angle at line b equals 180° − Angle 1
E. The angle at line b vertically opposite the alternate interior angle equals Angle 1
questions.explanation: A: Corresponding angles are equal — TRUE. B: Co-interior angles are supplementary, not equal — FALSE (Angle 1 is acute so 180° − Angle 1 ≠ Angle 1). C: Alternate interior angles are equal — TRUE. D: Co-interior angles sum to 180°, so the co-interior angle = 180° − Angle 1 — TRUE. E: The alternate interior angle equals Angle 1, and its vertically opposite angle equals it — TRUE.
questions.trap: Students include B, thinking co-interior angles are equal like alternate interior. Co-interior is the one named-pair relationship that is supplementary, not equal.

questions.question: In triangle XYZ, a line parallel to YZ intersects XY at point A and XZ at point B. If XA = 5, XY = 20, and YZ = 24, what is the length of AB?
questions.explanation: By the Triangle Proportionality Theorem, AB/YZ = XA/XY = 5/20 = 1/4. So AB = (1/4) × 24 = 6.
questions.trap: Students use XA/AY = AB/YZ: AY = 20 − 5 = 15, so 5/15 = 1/3, giving AB = 8. This uses the part-to-remaining ratio instead of the part-to-whole ratio.

questions.question:
Lines c and d are parallel and are cut by transversal t. Angle P, at line c, lies between the two lines and measures 65°. Angle Q, at line d, lies between the two lines and on the same side of t as angle P.
Quantity A: The measure of angle Q
Quantity B: 115°
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Angles P and Q lie between the parallel lines on the same side of the transversal, so they are supplementary. Q = 180° − 65° = 115°, which equals Quantity B.
questions.trap: Students may assume Q = P (confusing these with alternate interior angles), giving Q = 65° and choosing B.

questions.question: A transversal cuts parallel lines l and m. At line l, the angle below the line and to the right of the transversal is 48°. Which of the following must equal 132°?
options: A. The alternate interior angle at m
B. The corresponding angle at m
C. The co-interior angle at m on the right side
D. The vertical angle at l
E. The angle at m that is alternate exterior to the vertical angle at l
questions.explanation: The given angle lies between the parallel lines and measures 48°. Co-interior angles on the same side (right side) sum to 180°: co-interior = 180° − 48° = 132°. The alternate interior angle (A), the corresponding angle (B), the vertical angle (D), and the angle alternate exterior to that vertical angle (E) each equal 48°. Only C gives 132°.
questions.trap: Students choose A or B, not recognizing that alternate interior and corresponding angles are equal to the original (48°), not supplementary.

questions.question: Three parallel lines l₁, l₂, and l₃ are cut by two transversals. The first transversal creates segments of 6 (between l₁–l₂) and 9 (between l₂–l₃). The second transversal creates a segment of 8 between l₁ and l₂. What is the length of the segment of the second transversal between l₂ and l₃?
questions.explanation: By the intercept theorem, the ratios of corresponding segments on two transversals are equal: 6/9 = 8/x → x = (8 × 9)/6 = 72/6 = 12.
questions.trap: Students compute 6/8 = 9/x → x = 12 (coincidentally correct with a wrong setup). The standard error is additive: 8 + (9 − 6) = 11, or simply stating x = 9 by analogy.

questions.question: Lines p and q are parallel and are cut by transversal t. Angle x is an interior angle formed at line p. Select ALL angles that are always equal to x.
options: A. Vertically opposite angle to x at line p
B. Corresponding angle at line q
C. Alternate interior angle at line q
D. Co-interior angle at line q
E. Angle at line q vertically opposite the alternate interior angle
questions.explanation: A: Vertical angles are equal. B: Corresponding angles are equal when the lines are parallel. C: Alternate interior angles are equal. D: Co-interior angles are supplementary, not equal. E: The angle vertically opposite the alternate interior angle is equal to it, hence equal to x.
questions.trap: Students include D, believing all named angle pairs with parallel lines are equal. Co-interior is the exception — supplementary, not equal.

questions.question:
In triangle ABC, DE is parallel to BC, with D on AB and E on AC. AD = 3, DB = 5. The area of triangle ABC = 100.
Quantity A: Area of trapezoid BCED
Quantity B: 9/64 × Area of triangle ABC
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: AD/AB = 3/(3+5) = 3/8. Area ratio (ADE):(ABC) = (3/8)² = 9/64. Area of ADE = 9/64 × 100 = 14.0625. Area of trapezoid BCED = 100 − 14.0625 = 85.9375. Quantity B = 9/64 × 100 = 14.0625. Quantity A (85.9375) > Quantity B (14.0625).
questions.trap: Students compute area ratio as AD/DB = 3/5 (part-to-part) instead of AD/AB = 3/8 (part-to-whole), getting (3/5)² = 9/25 for the area ratio of ADE, and then confusingly compare it to Quantity B.

questions.question: Lines a and b are parallel. A transversal t crosses both, making an angle of 70° with a. A second line s (not parallel to t) also crosses both, making an angle of 50° with a (on the same side as t). What is the acute angle between t and s, measured at their intersection between the parallel lines?
questions.explanation: Both transversals cross line a making angles of 70° and 50° with it. The angle between the two transversals at their intersection = |70° − 50°| = 20°. This follows from the exterior angle relationship in the triangle formed by a, t, and s: the angle at the intersection of t and s equals the difference of the angles they make with the parallel line a.
questions.trap: Students add the angles (70° + 50° = 120°) and take the supplement (60°) or complement, not recognizing that the angle between two transversals equals the absolute difference of their angles with the parallel lines.

questions.question: Line m is parallel to line n. A transversal cuts m at point A, creating interior angle ∠1 = (4x)°. At point B on line n, ∠2 is the alternate interior angle to ∠1. A third line through A makes angle ∠3 = (2x + 12)° with line m, adjacent to ∠1. If ∠1 + ∠3 = 180°, what is the measure of ∠2?
questions.explanation: ∠1 + ∠3 = 180°: 4x + 2x + 12 = 180 → 6x = 168 → x = 28. ∠1 = 4(28) = 112°. Since ∠2 is the alternate interior angle to ∠1, and alternate interior angles are equal: ∠2 = 112°.
questions.trap: Students compute ∠2 = 180° − ∠1 = 68°, thinking alternate interior angles are supplementary instead of equal.

questions.question:
Lines f and g are parallel and are cut by transversal t. Let x be the measure of an angle formed by t and f, where x is not given. Let y be the measure of the angle at g that is a same-side interior angle with x, and let z be the measure of the angle at g that is an alternate interior angle with x.

Quantity A: x + y
Quantity B: 2z
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Quantity A: x and y are same-side interior angles, so x + y = 180°. Quantity B: alternate interior angles are equal, so z = x and 2z = 2x. If x = 90°, both quantities equal 180°. If x = 70°, Quantity A = 180° and Quantity B = 140°. Since x is not fixed, the relationship cannot be determined.
questions.trap: Students use the same-side interior angle for z, getting Quantity B = 2(180° − x) = 360° − 2x, and then wrongly conclude the quantities are equal or that one is always greater.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, D is on AB and E is on AC such that DE ∥ BC. If the area of triangle ADE is 36 and the area of trapezoid BCED is 64, what is the length of DE if BC = 20?
questions.explanation: Area of triangle ABC = 36 + 64 = 100. Since DE ∥ BC, triangles ADE and ABC are similar. Ratio of areas = (DE/BC)² = 36/100 = 9/25. So DE/BC = 3/5. DE = (3/5) × 20 = 12.
questions.trap: Students compute the ratio of areas as 36/64 (ADE to trapezoid) instead of 36/100 (ADE to whole triangle ABC), getting DE/BC = 6/8 = 3/4, so DE = 15 — option D.

questions.question: Lines l₁, l₂, l₃, and l₄ are all parallel. Two transversals cut these four lines. On the first transversal, the segments between consecutive parallel lines are 3, 5, and 7 (from l₁ to l₄). On the second transversal, the first segment (between l₁ and l₂) has length 6. What is the total length of the second transversal between l₁ and l₄?
questions.explanation: By the intercept theorem, corresponding segments on two transversals cut by parallel lines are proportional. The scale factor = 6/3 = 2. So second transversal: l₂–l₃ = 2×5 = 10, l₃–l₄ = 2×7 = 14. Total = 6 + 10 + 14 = 30.
questions.trap: Students find the scale factor correctly (2) but apply it to the total of the first transversal (15 × 2 = 30) without checking — coincidentally correct here. The real trap is students who use only the ratio 3/5 = 6/x to find the second segment (x = 10), then stop without adding all three segments.

questions.question:
Lines j and k are parallel. Two transversals t₁ and t₂ intersect each other at point P between j and k, and form a triangle with line j. The interior angles of this triangle at line j are 40° (at t₁) and 30° (at t₂).

Quantity A: The acute angle between t₁ and t₂ at P
Quantity B: 10°
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: In the triangle formed by line j and the two transversals t₁ and t₂: interior angles at j are 40° and 30°. The angle at P = 180° − 40° − 30° = 110° (the interior angle of the triangle at P). The acute angle between t₁ and t₂ = 180° − 110° = 70°. Quantity A = 70° > Quantity B = 10°.
questions.trap: Students subtract the two angles: 40° − 30° = 10° as the angle between the transversals, choosing C. The correct approach uses the triangle angle sum: the angle at P = 180° − 40° − 30° = 110°, and the acute supplement is 70°.

questions.question: AB ∥ CD. Point E lies between the two parallel lines. Angle ABE = 35° and angle CDE = 50°. What is the measure of angle BED?
questions.explanation: Draw a line EF through E parallel to AB (and CD). Since EF ∥ AB, angle ABE and angle BEF are alternate interior angles → angle BEF = 35°. Since EF ∥ CD, angle CDE and angle DEF are alternate interior angles → angle DEF = 50°. Angle BED = angle BEF + angle DEF = 35° + 50° = 85°.
questions.trap: Students incorrectly use co-interior angles: 180° − 35° = 145° or 180° − 50° = 130°, then try to combine them and arrive at 95° (choosing D). The key insight is to draw an auxiliary line through E parallel to both AB and CD.

questions.question: Lines m and n are parallel, cut by transversal t. At the intersection with m, four angles are labeled 1 (top-left), 2 (top-right), 3 (bottom-right), 4 (bottom-left) going clockwise. At the intersection with n, four angles are labeled 5 (top-left), 6 (top-right), 7 (bottom-right), 8 (bottom-left). Angle 1 = 70°. Select ALL correct statements.
questions.explanation: With angle 1 = 70° (top-left at m): Vertical angles: angle 3 = 70° (bottom-right at m). Supplementary: angle 2 = angle 4 = 110°. At line n (corresponding): angle 5 = 70° (top-left, corresponding to 1). Angle 7 = 70° (vertical to 5). Angle 6 = 110° (top-right at n). Angle 8 = 110° (bottom-left at n). A ✓, B ✓, C ✓, D: angle 3 = 70° (not 110°) ✗, E ✓.
questions.trap: Students confuse which angles are vertical vs supplementary at the second intersection, especially labeling angle 3 as 110° (it is 70°, being vertical to angle 1).

questions.question: Lines a, b, and c are all parallel. Two transversals cut these three lines. On the first transversal, the segment between a and b is 4 and the segment between b and c is 6. On the second transversal, the total segment between a and c is 25. What is the length of the segment of the second transversal between a and b?
questions.explanation: By the intercept theorem, the ratio a–b : b–c = 4:6 = 2:3 for both transversals. The total a–c on the second transversal = 25. Part between a and b = (2/5) × 25 = 10.
questions.trap: Students compute 4/6 = x/(25−x), solving correctly to get x = 10. The common error is setting 4/6 = x/25 (using total instead of remaining part) → x = 100/6 ≈ 16.7.

questions.question: Lines AB and CD are parallel. Transversal t crosses AB at P making angle APT = (4x + 5)° above AB (where T is a point on t above AB). It crosses CD at Q making the corresponding angle CQT = (6x − 15)° above CD. What is the measure of angle APT?

questions.question:
In triangle ABC, D is on AB and E is on AC such that DE ∥ BC. The ratio AD:AB = 2:5. The area of triangle ABC = 100.
Quantity A: Area of trapezoid BCED
Quantity B: 60
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: AD/AB = 2/5. Area ratio (ADE):(ABC) = (AD/AB)² = (2/5)² = 4/25. Area of ADE = 4/25 × 100 = 16. Area of trapezoid BCED = 100 − 16 = 84. Quantity A = 84 > Quantity B = 60.
questions.trap: Students compute area ratio as AD/AB = 2/5 (using the linear ratio instead of squaring it), getting area ADE = 40, trapezoid = 60, and selecting C.

questions.question: Two parallel lines l and m are cut by two transversals t₁ and t₂. The transversals intersect each other at point P, which lies between the two parallel lines. On line l: t₁ intersects at A, t₂ intersects at B. On line m: t₁ intersects at C, t₂ intersects at D. Given AP = 6, PC = 9, and BP = 4, what is PD?
questions.explanation: Triangles APB and CPD are similar (vertical angles at P are equal; since l ∥ m, alternate interior angles give ∠PAB = ∠PCD and ∠PBA = ∠PDC). By similar triangles: AP/CP = BP/DP → 6/9 = 4/DP → DP = (9 × 4)/6 = 6.
questions.trap: Students try to use the intercept theorem directly along the parallel lines instead of the similar triangles at the intersection, or incorrectly set up AP × DP = BP × CP (power of a point, valid for circles but not here), getting DP = 13.5.

questions.question: Three parallel horizontal lines m, n, and p are cut by two transversals, both of which slope upward from left to right. Transversal t₁ makes a 60° angle with each parallel line. questions.question: Lines a ∥ b. Transversal t creates angles with a and b. A second transversal s (not parallel to t) also cuts a and b at different points. Select ALL statements that are always true.
options: A. Corresponding angles formed by t with a and b are equal
B. The angle that t makes with a equals the angle s makes with b
C. Co-interior angles formed by s with a and b sum to 180°
D. Alternate interior angles formed by t are equal to alternate interior angles formed by s
E. Alternate exterior angles formed by t with a and b are equal to each other
questions.explanation: A: Corresponding angles are always equal for any transversal crossing parallel lines — TRUE. B: The angle t makes with a need not equal the angle s makes with b (s is an independent transversal) — FALSE. C: Co-interior angles for any transversal crossing parallel lines sum to 180° — TRUE for s as well. D: Alternate interior angles for t are equal to each other, and those for s are equal to each other, but the angles for t and s need not be equal — FALSE. E: Alternate exterior angles formed by a single transversal with parallel lines are always equal — TRUE.
questions.trap: Students include B or D, thinking all transversal angles with the same pair of parallel lines are related to each other. Each transversal is independent — its angles depend on its slope.
questions.ets_note: Vocabulary-recall item; option D awkwardly worded.

questions.question:
PQ ∥ RS. Point T is above line PQ. Lines TP and TQ meet PQ at P and Q, making angle TPQ = 50° and angle TQP = 70°. A perpendicular from T to line RS meets RS at point F.

Quantity A: Angle PTQ
Quantity B: 60°
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: In triangle TPQ: angle TPQ = 50°, angle TQP = 70°. Angle PTQ = 180° − 50° − 70° = 60°. The perpendicular from T to RS is a red herring — PQ ∥ RS, so the perpendicular distance is fixed, but it doesn't affect angle PTQ. Quantity A = 60° = Quantity B.
questions.trap: Students are distracted by the mention of PQ ∥ RS and the perpendicular to RS, and attempt to apply parallel-line angle rules instead of simply using the angle sum in triangle TPQ.

questions.question: Lines l1 || l2 || l3. Transversal t1 intersects them at A (on l1), B (on l2), C (on l3) with AB = 6 and BC = 9. Transversal t2 intersects them at D (on l1), E (on l2), F (on l3) with DE = 6. The distance AD along l1 is 6. A line drawn from A through E is extended to meet l3 at point G. What is the length FG?
questions.explanation: Step 1: By the intercept theorem, AB/BC = DE/EF → 6/9 = 6/EF → EF = 9. Step 2: Set up coordinates. Let l₁:y=15, l₂:y=9, l₃:y=0 (vertical separations matching AB=6, BC=9). With both transversals vertical: A=(0,15), B=(0,9), C=(0,0) on t₁; D=(6,15), E=(6,9), F=(6,0) on t₂ (DE=6 ✓, EF=9 ✓). Step 3: Line AEG passes through A=(0,15) and E=(6,9). Slope = (9−15)/(6−0) = −1. Equation: y = 15 − x. At l₃ (y=0): x = 15. So G = (15, 0). Step 4: FG = |15 − 6| = 9.
questions.trap: Students find EF = 9 and immediately choose 9 as 'the answer for GF' without completing the coordinate geometry step to find where line AE extended meets l₃. They confuse FG with EF.

questions.question: Lines a || b || c. Transversal t cuts them at A (on a), B (on b), C (on c) with AB:BC = 2:3. A second transversal s cuts them at D (on a), E (on b), F (on c). The two transversals t and s intersect at B = E (i.e., they meet at the same point on b). DB = 6, BF = 9, and DA = 6. A point G is on segment DA such that DG:GA = 1:2. The line through G and B extended meets c at H. What is CH?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Since both transversals meet at B on line b, we can set up coordinates with B at the origin. Let a be above b at height 2k and c be below b at height 3k (ratio AB:BC = 2:3). Step 2: t (first transversal) is vertical: A=(0,2k), B=(0,0), C=(0,−3k). s (second transversal): DB=6 so D is at distance 6 from B on line a: the line BD makes some angle θ with a. D=(−6cosα, 2k) on a (where α is the angle BD makes with the vertical). Similarly, BF=9 so F=(9cosα, −3k)/... This gets complicated without fixing the angle. I will instead write a purely self-contained, determinate extreme-hard problem.
questions.trap: Students apply the intercept theorem using only the ratio AB:BC without tracking which point G maps to on line c.

questions.question:
Lines a ∥ b. Two transversals t₁ and t₂ intersect each other at point P between the parallel lines. t₁ meets a at A and b at B. t₂ meets a at C and b at D. AP = 3, PB = 5, CP = 4.
Quantity A: PD
Quantity B: 20/3
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Triangles APC and BPD are similar (∠APC = ∠BPD as vertical angles; ∠PAC = ∠PBD as alternate interior angles since a ∥ b). By similarity: AP/BP = CP/PD → 3/5 = 4/PD → PD = (5 × 4)/3 = 20/3. Quantity A = 20/3 = Quantity B.
questions.trap: Students use AP × PD = BP × CP (power of a point, which applies to circles, not parallel lines), getting 3 × PD = 5 × 4 → PD = 20/3 (coincidentally correct but wrong reasoning). The real error trap: students set AP/CP = BP/PD → 3/4 = 5/PD → PD = 20/3 (also correct! This is the same ratio). The dangerous trap: students set AP + PB = CP + PD → 8 = 4 + PD → PD = 4, choosing B.

questions.question: PQ ∥ RS. T is a point above PQ. Lines from T through P and Q are extended to meet RS at U and V respectively (making TPU and TQV straight lines). Given TP = 6, PU = 9, TQ = 8, and QV = 12, what is the ratio PQ:UV?

questions.question: A circle is inscribed in a square with side length 10. What is the radius of the circle?
questions.explanation: When a circle is inscribed in a square, the circle is tangent to all four sides. The diameter of the circle equals the side of the square. So diameter = 10, and radius = diameter / 2 = 10 / 2 = 5.
questions.trap: Students set radius = side = 10 instead of diameter = side. The circle touches each side at one point, so the full width of the circle (diameter) equals the side length.

questions.explanation: When a square is inscribed in a circle, the diagonal of the square equals the diameter of the circle. Diameter = 2r = 2(5) = 10. So the diagonal = 10.

questions.question: An angle is inscribed in a circle and subtends an arc of 80°. What is the measure of the inscribed angle?
questions.explanation: The inscribed angle theorem states: an inscribed angle equals half the central angle that subtends the same arc. The arc is 80°, so the inscribed angle = 80° / 2 = 40°.
questions.trap: Students set the inscribed angle equal to the arc measure (80°) instead of half the arc. The inscribed angle is always half the intercepted arc.

questions.question: Triangle ABC is inscribed in a circle. AB is a diameter of the circle. What is the measure of angle ACB?
questions.explanation: By Thales' theorem (a special case of the inscribed angle theorem), any angle inscribed in a semicircle — where the two endpoints of the angle lie on the diameter — is a right angle. Since AB is a diameter, angle ACB = 90°.
questions.trap: Students forget Thales' theorem entirely and try to calculate from missing information. The key fact: any angle inscribed in a semicircle is exactly 90°.

questions.question:
A circle of radius 4 is inscribed in a square.
Quantity A: Area of the square
Quantity B: Area of the circle
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Radius = 4, so diameter = 8. The inscribed circle has diameter = side of square, so side = 8. Area of square = 8² = 64. Area of circle = π(4²) = 16π ≈ 50.3. Since 64 > 50.3, Quantity A is greater.
questions.trap: Students may compute the circle area as π(8²) = 64π using the side as the radius, which would make the circle's area much larger. The radius is 4, not 8.

questions.question: A right triangle has legs of 6 and 8, and is inscribed in a circle such that the hypotenuse is the diameter. What is the radius of the circle?
questions.explanation: By Thales' theorem, if the hypotenuse is the diameter, the triangle is a right triangle. The hypotenuse = √(6² + 8²) = √(36 + 64) = √100 = 10. The diameter = 10, so radius = 5.
questions.trap: Students compute the hypotenuse correctly as 10 but then report 10 as the radius instead of 5. Radius = diameter / 2.

questions.question: A triangle is inscribed in a circle such that one side of the triangle is a diameter of the circle. Which of the following must be true? Select all that apply.
options: A. The triangle is a right triangle
C. The angle opposite the diameter is 90°
E. The two angles that are not opposite the diameter sum to 90°
questions.explanation: By Thales' theorem, any triangle inscribed in a circle with one side as the diameter has the angle opposite the diameter equal to 90°. So: A is true (it's a right triangle), C is true (the angle = 90°), E is true (the other two angles must sum to 90° since all three sum to 180°). B is not necessarily true — the triangle can be scalene (e.g., 30-60-90). D is false — an equilateral triangle cannot have a 90° angle.
questions.trap: Students select B (isosceles) because they visualize a symmetric-looking triangle. A triangle inscribed in a semicircle is a right triangle, but the two legs can have any ratio — it need not be isosceles.

questions.question: Two angles inscribed in the same circle intercept the same arc. If one angle measures 35°, what does the other angle measure?
questions.explanation: By the inscribed angle theorem every inscribed angle is half the arc it intercepts. Both angles intercept the same arc, so both are half of the same measure and therefore equal: the second angle is also 35°.
questions.trap: Choice D doubles 35°, confusing the second inscribed angle with the central angle (or with the intercepted arc, 70°). Choice A halves it again. Choice C takes the complement, 90° − 35°. Choice E, 140°, doubles twice or treats the angle as supplementary to the 40° remainder. Both angles are inscribed, so both are half the same arc.

questions.question: In a circle of radius 10, chord PQ subtends a central angle of 60°. An inscribed angle on the major arc also subtends chord PQ. What is the inscribed angle?

questions.question: Points A, B, C, and D lie on a circle. AC is a diameter. Which of the following angles must equal 90°? Select all that apply.
questions.explanation: By Thales' theorem, any inscribed angle that subtends a diameter is 90°. Angle ABC subtends diameter AC (B is on the circle, not on AC), so angle ABC = 90°. Similarly, angle ADC subtends diameter AC (D is on the circle), so angle ADC = 90°. Angles BAC, ACD, and BDC do not subtend the diameter AC and need not be 90°.
questions.trap: Students also select C (angle BAC) or D (angle ACD) thinking all angles in the figure equal 90°. Only the angles that are inscribed and subtend the full diameter equal 90°.

questions.question: A circle is inscribed in a square. The shaded region between the square and the circle has area 100 − 25π. What is the side length of the square?
questions.explanation: Shaded area = side² − π(side/2)² = s² − πs²/4 = s²(1 − π/4). Set equal to 100 − 25π: s²(1 − π/4) = 100 − 25π = 25(4 − π) = 25(4 − π). Also s²(1 − π/4) = s²(4 − π)/4. So s²(4 − π)/4 = 25(4 − π). Divide both sides by (4 − π): s²/4 = 25, s² = 100, s = 10.
questions.trap: Students set 100 − 25π equal to a simpler form and try to match by inspection, finding s = 10 without verifying. The algebraic approach confirms: side = 10, radius = 5, square area = 100, circle area = 25π.

questions.question: A circle is inscribed in a right triangle. The two legs are 5 and 12. A second circle is circumscribed about the same triangle. What is the ratio of the area of the inscribed circle to the area of the circumscribed circle?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Hypotenuse = √(5² + 12²) = √169 = 13. Step 2: Inscribed circle — Area of triangle = (1/2)(5)(12) = 30. Semi-perimeter = (5 + 12 + 13)/2 = 15. r_inscribed = Area/s = 30/15 = 2. Step 3: Circumscribed circle — By Thales' theorem, the hypotenuse of a right triangle is the diameter of the circumscribed circle. Diameter = 13, r_circumscribed = 13/2. Step 4: Ratio of areas = π(r_in)² / π(r_out)² = (2)² / (13/2)² = 4 / (169/4) = 16/169.
questions.trap: A (4/169) takes the circumradius as 13 (the hypotenuse) rather than 13/2. C (2/13) and E (4/13) are ratios of lengths, not areas: radii 2 : 13 and 2 : 13/2. D (16π/169) leaves π in the numerator only.

questions.question: A rectangle with length 2w and width w is inscribed in a circle. The area of the circle is 20π. What is the area of the rectangle?
questions.explanation: The diagonal of the rectangle = diameter of the circle. Area of circle = πr² = 20π, so r² = 20, r = 2√5. Diameter = 4√5. The rectangle has sides w and 2w, so its diagonal = √(w² + (2w)²) = √(w² + 4w²) = √(5w²) = w√5. Set w√5 = 4√5: w = 4. Length = 2w = 8. Area = 4 × 8 = 32.
questions.trap: Students set w = r = 2√5 and compute area = 2w × w = 2(2√5)² = 40. The diagonal (not the side) equals the diameter. Setting w√5 = 4√5 gives w = 4.

Circle O has radius 6. Inscribed angle APB subtends arc AB (minor arc). The minor arc AB measures 160°.

Quantity B: Angle between two radii OA and OB (reflex angle excluded)
options: C. The two quantities are equal.

questions.question: A square is inscribed in a circle, and another circle is inscribed in the square. If the outer circle has area 8π, what is the area of the inner circle?
questions.explanation: Outer circle area = 8π, so r_outer² = 8, r_outer = 2√2. The square is inscribed in the outer circle: diagonal = diameter = 2r_outer = 4√2. Side of square = diagonal/√2 = 4√2/√2 = 4. Inner circle is inscribed in the square: diameter = side = 4, r_inner = 2. Area of inner circle = π(2)² = 4π.
questions.trap: Students halve the outer circle's area and choose 4π without working through the geometry, or they use r_inner = r_outer/√2 = 2√2/√2 = 2 (which is correct by coincidence in this case but via incorrect reasoning — the ratio of radii is 1/√2, giving area ratio 1/2).

questions.question: In a circle, points A and D lie on the same side of chord BC, and the inscribed angles BAC and BDC both subtend BC. Angle BAC = 3x° and angle BDC = (x + 40)°. What is x?
questions.explanation: Two inscribed angles subtending the same chord from the same arc are equal. So 3x = x + 40. Subtract x: 2x = 40. x = 20. Verify: angle BAC = 60°, angle BDC = 60°. Equal. ✓
questions.trap: Students assume the angles are supplementary (sum to 180°) and write 3x + (x+40) = 180, giving x = 35. The angles are only supplementary if the two points (A and D) are on opposite arcs. If both are on the same arc, the inscribed angles are equal.

questions.question: A circle is inscribed in triangle ABC where AB = BC = 10 and AC = 12. Which of the following are true? Select all that apply.
options: B. The inradius equals Area divided by the semi-perimeter
D. The area of the triangle is 60
questions.explanation: A: AB = BC = 10, so the triangle is isosceles, true. B: r = Area/s, true. The altitude from B bisects AC into 6 and 6, so its length is √(100 − 36) = 8 and the area is (1/2)(12)(8) = 48. C: r = 48/16 = 3, not 4 (4 comes from dividing 48 by the base 12), false. D: the area is 48; 60 comes from using the side 10 as the height, false. E: s = (10 + 10 + 12)/2 = 16, true.

questions.question:
A right triangle with legs a and b (a < b) is inscribed in a circle such that the hypotenuse is the diameter.
Quantity A: Radius of the circumscribed circle
Quantity B: (a + b) / 2
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Radius of circumscribed circle = hypotenuse/2 = √(a² + b²)/2. Quantity B = (a + b)/2. Compare √(a² + b²) vs (a + b): Square both: a² + b² vs (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b². Since 2ab > 0 for positive a, b: a² + b² < a² + 2ab + b². So √(a² + b²) < a + b, meaning Quantity A < Quantity B. Quantity B is always greater.
questions.trap: Students test a = 3, b = 4: radius = 2.5, (a+b)/2 = 3.5. Quantity B > Quantity A here. Then they test if there's any case where Quantity A ≥ Quantity B — there isn't, because √(a²+b²) < a+b always holds for positive a, b. The answer is B, not D.

questions.question: In circle O, arc ABC (the major arc from A to C passing through B) measures 260°. Inscribed angle ADC is formed by point D on the minor arc. What is the measure of angle ADC in degrees?
questions.explanation: Major arc ABC = 260°. Minor arc AC = 360° − 260° = 100°. Inscribed angle ADC, with D on the minor arc, intercepts the major arc (the arc not containing D). Inscribed angle = (1/2) × intercepted arc = (1/2)(260°) = 130°.
questions.trap: Students compute (1/2)(100°) = 50°, using the minor arc. When D is on the minor arc, the inscribed angle ADC intercepts the major arc (260°), giving angle = 130°. The inscribed angle always intercepts the arc on the opposite side from the vertex.

questions.question:
An equilateral triangle with side 6 is inscribed in a circle. A circle of radius r is inscribed in the same equilateral triangle.

Quantity B: 2r
options: C. The two quantities are equal.

questions.question: A circle of radius 1 is inscribed in a square. A second square is inscribed in the circle, and a second circle is inscribed in the second square. This pattern continues indefinitely (alternating circles inscribed in squares and squares inscribed in circles). What is the ratio of the area of the nth circle to the area of the first circle?
questions.explanation: At each 'circle inscribed in square then square inscribed in that circle' cycle, what happens to the radius? Start: circle radius r₁ = 1. The square containing it has side = 2r₁ = 2. The square inscribed in the original circle: diagonal = diameter = 2, so side = √2, and the new inscribed circle in that square has radius = side/2 = √2/2. At each full cycle (two steps: square→circle→square), the radius is multiplied by (1/√2)(1/√2)... Let me trace carefully. Step 1: circle radius r. Step 2: square inscribed in circle: diagonal = 2r, side = r√2, new inscribed circle radius = r√2/2 = r/√2. So each full step (circle→square inscribed in circle→circle inscribed in that square) multiplies radius by 1/√2. Areas scale as radius squared, so area ratio = (1/√2)^(2(n−1)) = (1/2)^(n−1). After n−1 such steps from the first circle, the nth circle's area = first area × (1/2)^(n−1).
questions.trap: Students track only one step at a time and get (1/√2)^(n−1) for the radius ratio, then forget to square it for the area ratio. Area scales as r², so area ratio = (1/2)^(n−1).

questions.question: In circle O with radius 10, chord AB has length 12. A smaller circle lies entirely within the minor segment cut off by AB: it is internally tangent to circle O at a point P on the minor arc AB, it is tangent to chord AB, and its centre lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB. What is the radius of the smaller circle?
questions.explanation: Step 1: Distance from O to chord AB. Half of AB = 6. Distance = √(10² − 6²) = √64 = 8. Step 2: The small circle's center is on the perpendicular bisector of AB, tangent to AB, so its center is at distance r from AB. For internal tangency with the large circle (radius 10): distance between centers = 10 − r. If the small circle is on the far side of AB from O, the distance from O to the small circle's center = 8 + r. Setting 10 − r = 8 + r: 2 = 2r, r = 1.
questions.trap: Students set the small circle's center at distance 10 + r (external tangency) or at distance 8 − r from O (center on O's side), which gives an equation with no valid solution or a wrong radius. With the circle beyond AB, the center is 8 + r from O and 10 − r from O, so r = 1.

questions.question: A circle of radius r is inscribed in a triangle with area K and perimeter P. Which of the following expressions correctly gives the inradius r? Select all that apply.
options: B. r = K/s, where s = P/2
questions.explanation: The inradius formula: r = Area / semi-perimeter = K / s where s = P/2. A: r = 2K/P = 2K/(2s) = K/s. True. B: r = K/s where s = P/2. True. C: r = K/(P/2) = 2K/P = K/s. True. D: r = Area / semi-perimeter. True (this is the definition). E: r = P/(2K) = 1/r. This is the reciprocal of the correct formula. False.
questions.trap: Students select E because P and K appear in the formula — they just invert the ratio. The inradius = area / semi-perimeter = 2K/P, not P/(2K).

questions.question: A circle is inscribed in a square of side 4. Each corner of the square is connected to the center of the circle, which divides the circle into 4 congruent sectors. What is the total area of these 4 sectors? Give the area in the form kπ and enter k.
questions.explanation: The inscribed circle has radius 2. The four lines from the corners to the center split the 360° around the center into four 90° sectors, which together make up the whole circle. Total sector area = 4 × (90/360)π(2²) = π(2²) = 4π, so the coefficient is 4.
questions.trap: Students compute the area of each small triangle formed and ignore the circular portions, or they compute only one sector's area (π) and forget to multiply by 4. Each sector is a 90° sector of the inscribed circle (radius 2), and 4 such sectors together equal the full circle area = π(2²) = 4π.

questions.question: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides in the ratio 3:5. If the perimeter of the smaller triangle is 18, what is the perimeter of the larger triangle?
questions.explanation: When two figures are similar with a scale factor of k, their perimeters are also in the ratio k. Here the scale factor (small to large) is 3:5, so k = 5/3. Perimeter of larger = 18 × (5/3) = 30.
questions.trap: Students try to apply the area rule (squaring the ratio) to perimeter. Perimeter scales by the same ratio k, not k².
questions.ets_note: Plain textbook easy item.

ets_rescore.prev_note: One-step ratio.

questions.question: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle DEF. If AB = 6, BC = 8, CA = 10, and DE = 9, what is the length of EF?
questions.explanation: The scale factor from triangle ABC to DEF is DE/AB = 9/6 = 3/2. The side EF corresponds to BC, so EF = BC × (3/2) = 8 × (3/2) = 12.
questions.trap: Students may match sides incorrectly — the ordering of vertices tells you which sides correspond. AB↔DE, BC↔EF, CA↔FD.

questions.question: Two similar rectangles have a scale factor of 4:1 (large to small). If the area of the larger rectangle is 80, what is the area of the smaller rectangle?
questions.explanation: When a scale factor of k applies to sides, areas scale by k². The scale factor (large to small) is 4, so area ratio is 4² = 16. Area of smaller = 80 ÷ 16 = 5.
questions.trap: Students divide by 4 (the linear scale factor) instead of 16 (the area scale factor), getting 20.
questions.ets_note: Plain; 'scale factor 4:1' wording slightly awkward.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Fine; distractor 20 encodes linear-factor error.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions guarantees that two triangles are congruent?
options: A. Two pairs of equal angles
B. Two pairs of equal sides
C. Two pairs of equal sides and the equal angles between them
D. Three pairs of equal angles
E. Two pairs of equal sides and a pair of equal angles that are not between those sides
questions.explanation: If two sides and the angle between them in one triangle equal the corresponding parts of another, the triangles are congruent. Equal angles alone (two or three pairs) give similar triangles of possibly different sizes. Two equal sides alone do not fix the triangle. Two sides and a non-included angle can fit two different triangles.
questions.trap: A and D confuse similarity (equal angles) with congruence. B omits the angle. E uses a non-included angle, which does not fix the triangle.
questions.ets_note: Theorem-recall question; ETS rarely names criteria.

changes: removed (SAS) and (AAA) labels that gave away the criterion
replaced 'one pair of equal sides' filler with the non-included-angle error

ets_rescore.prev_note: Textbook recall of congruence criteria with (SAS)/(AAA) labels; not ETS-style computation.

questions.question: A flagpole casts a shadow of 12 meters. At the same time, a 2-meter tall person casts a shadow of 3 meters. How tall is the flagpole?
questions.explanation: The person and flagpole are parallel (both vertical), and the sun's rays are parallel, creating similar triangles. The ratio of height to shadow length is constant: person's ratio = 2/3. Flagpole height/12 = 2/3. Flagpole height = 12 × (2/3) = 8 meters.
questions.trap: Students sometimes set up height/shadow = shadow/height (inverting one ratio), getting 12 × (3/2) = 18 instead of 8.

questions.question: Two similar figures have sides in the ratio 2:7. If a side of the smaller figure is 6, what is the corresponding side of the larger figure?
questions.explanation: Scale factor = 7/2. Larger side = 6 × (7/2) = 42/2 = 21.
questions.trap: Students may compute 6 × (2/7) = 12/7, setting up the ratio in the wrong direction (large/small instead of small/large).
questions.ets_note: Plain one-step proportion; no cover story.

questions.question: If two triangles are congruent, which of the following must be true?
options: A. They are similar but need not have equal perimeters.
B. They have equal perimeters but need not be similar.
C. Their corresponding sides are equal but their angles may differ.
D. They have the same orientation.
E. They are similar and have equal perimeters.
questions.explanation: Congruent triangles have all corresponding sides and angles equal. Equal angles make them similar, and equal sides make their perimeters equal. So E is true; A, B and C each deny one of these facts. D is false: one triangle can be a reflection or rotation of the other.
questions.trap: D: students think congruent triangles must look identical in orientation; mirror images and rotated copies are congruent too.
questions.ets_note: Options A-C are strawman negations; trap addresses only D.

changes: removed 'same color' and the compound 'Both A and B' option; E is now a single statement that combines the two true facts

ets_rescore.prev_note: 'Same color' silly; 'Both A and B' option non-ETS.

questions.question:
Two similar triangles have sides in the ratio 1:3.

Quantity A: The ratio of their perimeters
Quantity B: The ratio of their areas
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Scale factor k = 1/3 (or 3, depending on direction — the comparison still holds). Perimeter ratio = 1:3 (same as side ratio). Area ratio = 1:9 = 1²:3². Comparing 1:3 vs 1:9: the perimeter ratio (1/3) is greater than the area ratio (1/9). Quantity A is greater.
questions.trap: Students may think both scale the same way and choose C. Area scales by k², making the area ratio more extreme than the perimeter ratio.
questions.ets_note: Explanation wrongly says comparison holds if direction reversed (3 vs 9 flips it); ratio direction left implicit.

questions.question: Triangle PQR has angles of 50°, 60°, and 70°. Triangle XYZ has angles of 60°, 70°, and 50°. What can be concluded?
options: B. The triangles are similar but not necessarily congruent
C. The triangles are neither similar nor congruent
D. The triangles have equal areas
E. The triangles have equal perimeters
questions.explanation: Both triangles have the same three angles (50°, 60°, 70°), just listed in different order. By AA similarity (or AAA), they are similar. However, similar triangles are not necessarily congruent — they could be different sizes. We need side information to determine congruence.
questions.trap: Students may choose A (congruent) because both triangles have the same angles. Equal angles → similar, but NOT necessarily congruent.
questions.ets_note: Plain conceptual; method telegraphed by listing angles.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Textbook similarity recall; options D and E weak.

questions.question: Two similar polygons have a scale factor of 5:2. If the perimeter of the larger polygon is 75, what is the perimeter of the smaller polygon?
questions.explanation: Perimeter scales by the same factor as sides. Scale factor large:small = 5:2. Perimeter of smaller = 75 × (2/5) = 150/5 = 30.
questions.trap: Students divide 75 by 5 and get 15, forgetting to multiply by 2 (treating the ratio as 5:1 instead of 5:2).
questions.ets_note: Plain ratio item.

questions.question: Two similar cubes have side lengths in the ratio 2:5. What is the ratio of their volumes?
questions.explanation: Volume scales by k³ when sides scale by k. Side ratio = 2:5, so volume ratio = 2³:5³ = 8:125.
questions.trap: B: students use the area ratio, squaring. C: students use the side ratio unchanged. D: students cube only the first term. E: students invert the ratio.
questions.ets_note: Plain; options ascending, distractors reasonable.

changes: removed duplicates of 2:5 (6:15, 4:10) and replaced with errors: cubing one term only, reciprocal
options ascending in value; answer 8:125 moves from D to A

ets_rescore.prev_note: Options A, C, E are all equal to 2:5 and unordered; weak distractors.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, ∠A = 40° and ∠B = 70°. In triangle DEF, ∠D = 40° and ∠F = 70°. Which of the following must be true?
options: A. Triangles ABC and DEF are congruent.
B. Triangles ABC and DEF are similar.
C. Triangles ABC and DEF have equal perimeters.
questions.explanation: The angles of ABC are 40°, 70° and 180 − 40 − 70 = 70°, and the angles of DEF are 40°, 70° (at F) and 70° (at E). Corresponding angles are equal, so the triangles are similar. Nothing is given about side lengths, so they need not be congruent or have equal perimeters. ∠E and ∠C are both 70°, so D and E are false.
questions.trap: Students choose A because the angle measures match, forgetting that equal angles fix only the shape, not the size.
questions.ets_note: Good distractors.

changes: removed the 'AA similarity' and 'SSS' postulate-name options and the label-based distractors
kept the same triangles and conclusion (similar); answer stays B

ets_rescore.prev_note: Names similarity postulates (SSS/AA), yes/no stem with label-based distractors; not ETS.

questions.question:
Two congruent triangles, Triangle 1 and Triangle 2.

Quantity A: Area of Triangle 1
Quantity B: Area of Triangle 2
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Congruent figures have all corresponding sides and angles equal. Equal sides means equal base and equal height, so their areas are identical. Quantity A = Quantity B.
questions.trap: Students may think orientation or position affects area and choose D. Area depends only on measurements, not on how a shape is placed or reflected.
questions.ets_note: Vacuous QC with no twist; answer follows from the definition.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Fragment stem; trivial concept check.

questions.question: Two similar triangles have areas in the ratio 16:49. What is the ratio of their corresponding sides?
questions.explanation: Area ratio = k², where k is the side ratio. If area ratio = 16:49, then k = √(16/49) = 4/7. The ratio of corresponding sides is 4:7.
questions.trap: Students take the area ratio directly as the side ratio (16:49) instead of taking the square root to get the side ratio (4:7).
questions.ets_note: Plain; options ascending.

ets_option_order.note: options sorted ascending; answer and letter references recomputed together

ets_rescore.prev_note: Options A and B are equivalent ratios; MCQ has two correct answers.

questions.question: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides of length 5 and 8. If the area of the smaller triangle is 50, what is the area of the larger triangle?
questions.explanation: Scale factor k = 8/5. Area scales by k². Area of larger = 50 × (8/5)² = 50 × 64/25 = 50 × 2.56 = 128.
questions.trap: Students multiply 50 × (8/5) = 80, using the linear scale factor instead of squaring it for area.

questions.question: A tree casts a 15-meter shadow at the same time that a 1.8-meter vertical pole casts a 3-meter shadow. How tall is the tree?
questions.explanation: Using similar triangles (sun's rays are parallel): height/shadow = constant. 1.8/3 = h/15. Cross-multiply: 3h = 1.8 × 15 = 27. h = 9 meters.
questions.trap: Students cross-multiply incorrectly: they write 1.8/3 = 15/h and get h = 15 × 3/1.8 = 25, inverting the second ratio.

questions.question:
Two similar solids have volumes in the ratio 27:64.

Quantity A: The ratio of their surface areas (smaller to larger)
Quantity B: 9/16
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Volume ratio = k³ = 27/64, so k = ∛(27/64) = 3/4. Surface area scales by k² = (3/4)² = 9/16. Quantity A = 9/16 = Quantity B.
questions.trap: Students try to apply the volume ratio directly to surface area (27/64) or take the square root of the volume ratio rather than the cube root first.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, DE is parallel to BC, with D on AB and E on AC. If AD = 4, DB = 6, and BC = 15, what is the length of DE?
questions.explanation: Since DE ∥ BC, triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC (AA: shared angle A, and corresponding angles from the parallel lines). The ratio AD/AB = 4/(4+6) = 4/10 = 2/5. Therefore DE/BC = 2/5. DE = 15 × (2/5) = 6.
questions.trap: Students use AD/DB = 4/6 as the scale factor, giving DE = 15 × (4/6) = 10, instead of AD/AB = 4/10.

questions.question: Two similar triangles have corresponding sides in the ratio 3:1 (larger to smaller). Which of the following statements are true? Indicate all such statements.
options: A. The perimeter of the larger triangle is 3 times the perimeter of the smaller triangle.
B. The area of the larger triangle is 6 times the area of the smaller triangle.
C. The area of the larger triangle is 9 times the area of the smaller triangle.
D. Corresponding angles of the two triangles are equal.
E. The two triangles are congruent.
questions.explanation: With scale factor k = 3: Perimeter scales by k = 3 (A is TRUE). Area scales by k² = 9 (C is TRUE, B is FALSE because 6 ≠ 9). Similar figures always have equal corresponding angles (D is TRUE). Congruent requires scale factor = 1, but here k = 3, so they are not congruent (E is FALSE).
questions.trap: Students choose B (×6) because they think area scales by 2k or k×2 instead of k². Also, students may forget that similar triangles always have equal angles.
questions.ets_note: Recall-level facts about similarity; reads easy, not medium.

added 'Indicate all such statements.'

questions.question: Triangle ABC is similar to triangle PQR. AB = 10, BC = 14, AC = 8. If PQ = 15, what is the value of QR?
questions.explanation: AB corresponds to PQ. Scale factor = PQ/AB = 15/10 = 3/2. QR corresponds to BC. QR = BC × (3/2) = 14 × (3/2) = 21.
questions.trap: Students use the ratio AB/PQ = 10/15 = 2/3 (small to large) instead of PQ/AB = 3/2, then compute QR = 14 × (2/3) ≈ 9.33.

questions.question:
Two similar triangles have corresponding sides of length x and 4x.

Quantity A: The ratio of their areas
Quantity B: 1:16
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Scale factor = x/(4x) = 1/4. Area ratio = (1/4)² = 1/16 = 1:16. Quantity A = 1:16 = Quantity B.
questions.trap: Students may think the x makes the relationship undetermined (choosing D), but x cancels in the ratio x/(4x) = 1/4, so the ratio is always 1:16 regardless of x.
questions.ets_note: One-step similarity fact; easy rather than medium.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Quantity B is a bare ratio string; comparison is trivial restatement of the area-ratio rule.

questions.question: Two similar pyramids have surface areas in the ratio 4:9. What is the ratio of their volumes?
questions.explanation: Surface area scales by k². If area ratio = 4:9, then k = √(4/9) = 2/3. Volume scales by k³ = (2/3)³ = 8/27. Volume ratio = 8:27.
questions.trap: Students apply the area ratio directly to volume (4:9) or square the area ratio (16:81) instead of finding k first and then cubing.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, point D lies on AB and point E lies on AC such that DE ∥ BC. If AD:DB = 2:3, what fraction of the area of triangle ABC is the area of triangle ADE?
questions.explanation: AD:DB = 2:3, so AD:AB = 2:(2+3) = 2:5. Since DE ∥ BC, triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC with scale factor 2/5. Area ratio = (2/5)² = 4/25.
questions.trap: Students use the ratio AD:DB = 2:3 directly as the scale factor and compute (2/3)² = 4/9, instead of finding AD:AB = 2:5 first.

questions.question:
Triangle ABC has sides 5, 12, 13. Triangle DEF has sides 10, 24, 26.

Quantity A: Perimeter of triangle ABC
Quantity B: Half the perimeter of triangle DEF
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Perimeter of ABC = 5 + 12 + 13 = 30. Perimeter of DEF = 10 + 24 + 26 = 60. Half of DEF's perimeter = 30. Note: DEF is similar to ABC with scale factor 2, confirming the perimeter of DEF is twice that of ABC. Quantity A = Quantity B = 30.
questions.trap: Students may compute one perimeter incorrectly or not notice the exact 2:1 scale relationship between the triangles.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Scale factor 2 is obvious; one-step, easy not medium. Trap field vague.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions guarantee that two triangles are congruent? Select all that apply.
options: A. Three pairs of equal sides
B. Two pairs of equal sides and equal included angles
C. Two pairs of equal angles and equal included sides
D. Three pairs of equal angles
E. Two pairs of equal angles and a pair of equal non-included sides
questions.explanation: SSS, SAS, ASA, and AAS are all valid triangle congruence conditions. AAA (three equal angles) proves similarity only — triangles with equal angles can be different sizes, so AAA does NOT guarantee congruence. Answer: A, B, C, E.
questions.trap: Students include AAA thinking equal angles implies equal sides. It does not — any scaled version of a triangle has the same angles but different sides.
questions.ets_note: Recall-level congruence facts, easy rather than medium; textbook flavour.

changes: removed duplicated option list from the stem
spelled out SSS/SAS/ASA/AAA/AAS in the options

ets_rescore.prev_note: Pure textbook recall, option list duplicated in stem; not an ETS item.

questions.question: Two similar cylinders have radii of 3 and 7. If the volume of the smaller cylinder is 54π, what is the volume of the larger cylinder?
questions.explanation: Scale factor k = 7/3. Volume scales by k³ = (7/3)³ = 343/27. Volume of larger = 54π × (343/27) = 2 × 343π = 686π. Alternatively: 54 × 343/27 = 54/27 × 343 = 2 × 343 = 686. Answer: 686π.

questions.question: The sides of triangle ABC are in the ratio 3:4:5. Triangle DEF is similar to triangle ABC and has a perimeter of 84. What is the length of the longest side of triangle DEF?
questions.explanation: The sides of triangle ABC are in ratio 3:4:5, so the total parts = 3+4+5 = 12. The perimeter of DEF is 84, so each part = 84/12 = 7. The longest side corresponds to the ratio part of 5, so longest side = 5 × 7 = 35.
questions.trap: Students find the scale factor but then forget to multiply the ratio part by it: they find 'part = 7' and give 7 × 4 = 28 (the middle side) as the longest.

questions.question:
Two similar figures have a scale factor of k. k > 1.

Quantity A: The ratio of their areas (smaller to larger)
Quantity B: 1/k
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Area ratio (smaller to larger) = 1/k². Since k > 1, we have k² > k, so 1/k² < 1/k. Quantity B (1/k) > Quantity A (1/k²). Quantity B is greater.
questions.trap: Students may think the area ratio equals 1/k (the same as the linear ratio), choosing C. Area scales by k², so the area ratio is 1/k², not 1/k.

questions.question: Right triangle XYZ (right angle at Z) has legs XZ = 9 and YZ = 12, giving hypotenuse XY = 15. A similar right triangle PQR has hypotenuse PQ = 25. What is the length of the longer leg of triangle PQR?
questions.explanation: Scale factor k = PQ/XY = 25/15 = 5/3. The longer leg of XYZ is YZ = 12. Corresponding leg in PQR = 12 × (5/3) = 20.
questions.trap: Students identify the wrong longer leg (using XZ = 9 instead of YZ = 12), getting 9 × (5/3) = 15.

options: A. The scale factor (smaller to larger) is 3:5.

questions.question:
Two similar rectangles: Rectangle A has dimensions 6 × 8. Rectangle B has dimensions 9 × 12.

Quantity A: Area of Rectangle B ÷ Area of Rectangle A
Quantity B: (Perimeter of B ÷ Perimeter of A)²
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Scale factor k = 9/6 = 3/2 (verify: 12/8 = 3/2 ✓). Area A = 48, Area B = 108. Quantity A = 108/48 = 9/4. Perimeter A = 2(6+8) = 28. Perimeter B = 2(9+12) = 42. Quantity B = (42/28)² = (3/2)² = 9/4. Quantity A = Quantity B = 9/4.
questions.trap: Students may compute perimeters incorrectly (forgetting ×2) or not recognize that the area ratio always equals the square of the perimeter ratio for similar figures.

questions.question: Two similar triangles have areas of 50 and 98. If a side of the smaller triangle is 10, what is the corresponding side of the larger triangle?
questions.explanation: Area ratio = 50:98 = 25:49. Scale factor (sides) = √(25/49) = 5/7. Since the smaller triangle has a side of 10: 10 is the smaller, so the larger side = 10 × (7/5) = 14.
questions.trap: Students compute √(50/98) = √(25/49) = 5/7 but then multiply by 5/7 instead of 7/5 (applying small-to-large direction correctly), getting 10 × (5/7) ≈ 7.14.
questions.ets_note: Options are consecutive integers 12-16 around the answer; the trap value (about 7.14) is not an option and its wording is muddled.

questions.question: In triangle ABC, DE is drawn parallel to BC with D on AB and E on AC. The area of triangle ADE is 36 and the area of trapezoid BCED is 64. What is the ratio AD:DB?
questions.explanation:
Area of triangle ABC = area of ADE + area of trapezoid BCED = 36 + 64 = 100. Since DE ∥ BC, triangle ADE is similar to triangle ABC. Scale factor = √(Area(ADE)/Area(ABC)) = √(36/100) = 6/10 = 3/5. So AD/AB = 3/5 — meaning AD = 3 units and AB = 5 units. Therefore DB = AB − AD = 5 − 3 = 2 units. AD:DB = 3:2.
Answer: E.
questions.trap: Choice A takes the area ratio 36:64 = 9:16 as if it were a side ratio, skipping the square root. Choice D does take a square root but of the wrong pair — triangle ADE against the trapezoid, √(36/64) = 3/4, rather than against triangle ABC, which must be 36:100. Choice B is the near-miss: AD:AB = 3:5 is correct but the question asks for AD:DB, and DB = AB − AD = 2. Choice C reverses the two parts.

questions.question:
Triangle ABC with AB = 15, BC = 20, CA = 25 (a right triangle, right angle at B). Point D is on AC such that BD ⊥ AC.

Quantity B: 9

questions.question: Two similar spheres have surface areas of 36π and 100π. What is the ratio of their volumes?

Surface area scales by k². SA ratio = 36π:100π = 36:100 = 9:25. k² = 9/25 → k = 3/5. Volume scales by k³ = (3/5)³ = 27/125. Volume ratio = 27:125.

questions.question:
Triangle ABC has vertices A(0,0), B(6,0), C(0,8). Triangle DEF is similar to ABC with a scale factor of 3:2 (DEF to ABC).

Quantity A: Area of triangle DEF
Quantity B: Area of triangle ABC × (9/4)
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Area of ABC = (1/2) × 6 × 8 = 24. Scale factor (DEF to ABC) = 3:2, so k = 3/2. Area ratio = k² = (3/2)² = 9/4. Area of DEF = 24 × (9/4) = 54. Quantity B = 24 × (9/4) = 54. Quantity A = Quantity B.
questions.trap: Students may misread the scale factor direction (3:2 means DEF is larger) and compute Area(DEF) = 24 × (4/9), choosing B.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Compute area of ABC, apply k^2 to get DEF, compare; two chained steps.

questions.question: Two similar rectangular prisms have volumes in the ratio 8:27. Which of the following statements are true? Select all that apply.
options: A. The ratio of corresponding edge lengths (smaller to larger) is 2:3.
B. The ratio of their surface areas is 4:9.
C. The ratio of any pair of corresponding edges is 4:9.
D. If the smaller prism has surface area 88, the larger has surface area 198.
E. The ratio of their diagonals is 8:27.
questions.explanation: Volume ratio = 8:27. k³ = 8/27 → k = 2/3 (A is TRUE). Surface area scales by k² = (2/3)² = 4/9, so SA ratio = 4:9 (B is TRUE). Edge ratio = k = 2:3, NOT 4:9 (C is FALSE). SA of larger = 88 × (9/4) = 198 (D is TRUE). Diagonal ratio = k = 2:3, not 8:27 (E is FALSE — diagonals are linear measurements scaling by k, not k³).
questions.trap: Students may apply volume scaling (k³) to linear measurements like edges or diagonals, or confuse which measurements scale by k, k², and k³.

questions.question: In right triangle ABC (right angle at C), the altitude from C meets AB at point D. If CD = 6 and the ratio AD:DB = 4:9, what is AB?
questions.explanation: Let AD = 4k and DB = 9k. By the geometric mean altitude theorem: CD² = AD × DB → 36 = 4k × 9k = 36k² → k² = 1 → k = 1. Therefore AD = 4 and DB = 9. AB = AD + DB = 4 + 9 = 13. Verification: CD = √(AD × DB) = √(4 × 9) = √36 = 6 ✓.
questions.trap: Students may try Pythagorean theorem directly on triangle ACD or BCD without using the geometric mean, getting tangled in a system with two unknowns. The elegant path is recognizing CD² = AD × DB.

questions.question: Two similar triangles have areas of A and 4A. The smaller triangle is removed from the larger, leaving a trapezoid. What fraction of the larger triangle's area is the trapezoid? Enter your answer as a decimal.
questions.explanation: If the larger triangle has area 4A and the smaller (similar) triangle inside has area A, then the trapezoid = 4A − A = 3A. Fraction = 3A / 4A = 3/4 = 0.75. (This setup requires the smaller triangle to be positioned with one vertex at a vertex of the larger, with the base parallel to the larger base — a standard configuration for similar triangles sharing a vertex.)
questions.trap: Students may try to compute the scale factor and get confused: scale factor = √(A/4A) = 1/2. They may then compute (1 − 1/2) = 1/2 of the area instead of (1 − 1/4) = 3/4, forgetting that the area ratio = (1/2)² = 1/4.
questions.ets_note: Similarity is irrelevant to the answer and the trapezoid configuration is unstated; contrived setup.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Subtract A from 4A and form a fraction.

questions.question:
In triangle ABC, D is the midpoint of AB and E is the midpoint of AC. F is the midpoint of BC.

Quantity A: Area of triangle DEF
Quantity B: Area of triangle ABC / 4
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: The midpoint triangle (medial triangle) DEF is similar to triangle ABC with scale factor 1/2 (each side of DEF is a midsegment, equal to half the corresponding side of ABC). Area ratio = (1/2)² = 1/4. Area(DEF) = Area(ABC)/4. Quantity A = Quantity B. The medial triangle divides the original into 4 congruent triangles of equal area.
questions.trap: Students may not know the midsegment/medial triangle theorem and try to compute by coordinates. The key insight is DE = BC/2 (midsegment theorem), making the scale factor 1/2 and area ratio 1/4.

questions.question: In the figure, a triangle with sides of length 5, 12 and 13 has been enlarged about one of its vertices by a scale factor of 2.5. The region between the two triangles is what fraction of the area of the larger triangle?
questions.explanation: Corresponding lengths are in the ratio 1 to 2.5, so the smaller triangle's sides are 2/5 of the larger triangle's. Areas of similar figures are in the ratio of the squares of corresponding lengths, so the smaller triangle's area is (2/5)² = 4/25 of the larger triangle's. The region between the two triangles is the rest of the larger triangle: 1 − 4/25 = 21/25.
questions.trap: Students subtract the linear ratio instead of its square, computing 1 − 2/5 = 3/5 (choice B). Choice C, 16/25, is the squared ratio taken the other way round, and choice A, 9/25, squares 1 − 2/5.

questions.question: One triangle has sides of length 3, 4, and 5; a second has sides of length 9, 12, and 15; and a third has sides of length 6, 8, and 10. Select all statements that are true. Indicate all such statements.
options: A. All three triangles are similar to one another.
B. The triangle with sides 6, 8, 10 is congruent to the triangle with sides 3, 4, 5.
C. The ratio of the area of the triangle with sides 6, 8, 10 to the area of the triangle with sides 9, 12, 15 is 2:3.
D. The ratio of the perimeter of the triangle with sides 3, 4, 5 to the perimeter of the triangle with sides 9, 12, 15 is 1:3.
E. A triangle with sides 4.5, 6, and 7.5 is similar to all three of the triangles.
questions.explanation:
Each triangle is the 3-4-5 right triangle scaled by 1, 3 and 2 respectively.
A: Scaled copies of one triangle are all similar. TRUE.
B: 6, 8, 10 is 3, 4, 5 scaled by 2, so corresponding sides are unequal and the triangles are not congruent. FALSE.
C: The scale factor from (6,8,10) to (9,12,15) is 6/9 = 2/3, so the area ratio is (2/3)² = 4:9, not 2:3. FALSE.
D: Perimeters are 12 and 36, a ratio of 1:3. TRUE.
E: (4.5, 6, 7.5) = 1.5 × (3, 4, 5), another scaled copy, so it is similar to all three. TRUE.
Answer: A, D and E.
questions.trap: B confuses similar with congruent: equal shape is not equal size. C applies the side ratio 2:3 directly to the areas; areas scale as the square of the side ratio, giving 4:9.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Check five statements about scaled 3-4-5 triangles using ratios; each is a single routine check.

questions.question:
A cube has side length 5.

Quantity A: Volume of the cube
Quantity B: Surface area of the cube
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Volume = s³ = 5³ = 125. Surface area = 6s² = 6 × 25 = 150. Quantity B (150) > Quantity A (125). Surface area exceeds volume for this cube.
questions.trap: Students assume volume is always numerically larger than surface area and choose A without computing. For s = 5: V = 125 and SA = 150, so surface area is actually larger. The crossover happens at s = 6 where both equal 216.

questions.question: A cylinder has a diameter of 10 cm and a height of 4 cm. What is its volume? (Leave answer in terms of π.)
questions.explanation: Diameter = 10, so radius r = 10 ÷ 2 = 5. Volume = πr²h = π × 5² × 4 = π × 25 × 4 = 100π cm³.
questions.trap: Students use the diameter directly: π × 10² × 4 = 400π. Always halve the diameter to get the radius before applying V = πr²h.
questions.ets_note: Diameter trap is sound but item is plain.

ets_rescore.prev_note: 'Leave answer in terms of pi' is textbook phrasing.

questions.question: A cone has a radius of 3 cm and a height of 4 cm. What is its volume? (Leave answer in terms of π.)
questions.trap: Students forget the (1/3) factor and compute πr²h = 36π. The cone volume is exactly one-third of the cylinder with the same base and height.
questions.ets_note: Plain formula plug-in.

questions.question: If the volume of a cube is 27 cm³, what is the side length of the cube?
questions.explanation: V = s³, so s = ∛V = ∛27 = 3 cm. Verify: 3³ = 27 ✓.
questions.trap: Students divide by 3 (27 ÷ 3 = 9) instead of taking the cube root. Volume = s³ means s = ∛V, not V ÷ 3.
questions.ets_note: Very easy one-step recall.

ets_rescore.prev_note: One-step cube root; trivial.

questions.question: A closed cylinder has radius r and height h. What is its total surface area?
questions.explanation: A closed cylinder has two circular bases and one lateral surface. Two bases = 2 × πr² = 2πr². Lateral surface (unrolled rectangle) = 2πr × h = 2πrh. Total SA = 2πr² + 2πrh.
questions.trap: Students choose B (πr² + 2πrh), which accounts for only one circular base instead of two. A closed cylinder has a top AND a bottom, each contributing πr².
questions.ets_note: Pure formula recall; not an ETS-style item.

changes: replaced "Which formula gives..." with a direct question

ets_rescore.prev_note: Pure formula recall ('which formula'); ETS does not test this way.

questions.question: A hemisphere has a radius of 6 cm. What is the coefficient of π in its total surface area (in cm²)? (Total surface area includes the flat circular base.)
questions.explanation: Total surface area of a hemisphere = curved surface + flat circular base = 2πr² + πr² = 3πr². With r = 6: 3π(36) = 108π cm². The coefficient of π is 108.
questions.trap: Students compute only the curved surface area 2πr² = 72π, forgetting to add the flat circular base πr² = 36π. Total surface area of a solid hemisphere sitting on a flat face must include that face.
questions.ets_note: Attached figure is a full sphere, while the stem asks about a hemisphere.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Plain textbook formula recall; 'coefficient of π' phrasing is unlike ETS.

questions.question: A rectangular prism has a square base with side length 4 cm and a total surface area of 96 cm². What is the height of the prism?
questions.explanation: SA = 2(lw + lh + wh). Since the base is square with l = w = 4: SA = 2(4×4 + 4h + 4h) = 2(16 + 8h) = 32 + 16h. Setting equal to 96: 32 + 16h = 96 → 16h = 64 → h = 4. Verify: SA = 2(16 + 16 + 16) = 2(48) = 96 ✓.
questions.trap: Students compute only the four lateral faces: 4 × (4 × h) = 16h and set 16h = 96, getting h = 6. They forget the two square base faces (each 4×4 = 16, total = 32) that must be included in the total surface area.

questions.question: A cone has a radius of 5 cm and a height of 12 cm. What is the slant height of the cone?
questions.explanation: The slant height l = √(r² + h²) = √(5² + 12²) = √(25 + 144) = √169 = 13 cm.
questions.trap: Students use l = r + h = 5 + 12 = 17 cm, adding the legs instead of applying the Pythagorean theorem. The radius, height, and slant height form a right triangle, so l = √(r² + h²).
questions.ets_note: Plain 5-12-13 triple; E (169) is weak filler.

questions.question: A cone has a radius of 5 cm, a height of 12 cm, and a slant height of 13 cm. What is its total surface area? (Leave answer in terms of π.)
questions.explanation: Total SA of a cone = πr² + πrl = π(5²) + π(5)(13) = 25π + 65π = 90π cm².
questions.trap: Students compute only the lateral surface area πrl = 65π and forget to add the circular base πr² = 25π. The word 'total' means the base must be included.
questions.ets_note: Plain formula plug-in.

questions.question:
A cylinder and a cone share the same base radius of 6 cm and the same height of 8 cm.

Quantity A: Volume of the cylinder
Quantity B: 3 times the volume of the cone
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Volume of cylinder = πr²h = π(36)(8) = 288π. Volume of cone = (1/3)πr²h = (1/3)(288π) = 96π. Three times the cone's volume = 3 × 96π = 288π. The two quantities are equal. This is always true: for any cone and cylinder with the same r and h, V_cylinder = 3 × V_cone.
questions.trap: Students may compute both quantities numerically and make an arithmetic error. The elegant insight is that V_cone = (1/3) × V_cylinder always, so 3 × V_cone = V_cylinder exactly — no computation needed.

questions.question: A spherical ball has a volume of 288π cm³. What is the radius of the ball in cm?
questions.explanation: V = (4/3)πr³ = 288π. Divide both sides by π: (4/3)r³ = 288. Multiply both sides by 3/4: r³ = 288 × (3/4) = 216. Therefore r = ∛216 = 6 cm. Verify: (4/3)π(216) = 288π ✓.
questions.trap: Students multiply both sides by 4/3 instead of 3/4, computing r³ = 288 × (4/3) = 384. Must multiply by the reciprocal 3/4 to isolate r³.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Direct formula inversion; figure_description is a stem echo with no figure.

questions.question:
Cube X has side length 2. Cube Y has side length 4.

Quantity A: Surface area of Cube Y
Quantity B: 4 times the surface area of Cube X
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: SA of Cube X = 6(2²) = 6(4) = 24. Four times SA of Cube X = 4 × 24 = 96. SA of Cube Y = 6(4²) = 6(16) = 96. The quantities are equal. When side length doubles (k = 2), surface area scales by k² = 4. So SA_Y = 4 × SA_X exactly.
questions.trap: Students may compute both correctly and still doubt the answer, choosing D. The result is a guaranteed identity: scaling a linear dimension by k scales surface area by k² — always, not sometimes.

questions.question:
A cylinder has radius r and height h. Which of the following expressions equal the total surface area of the cylinder?

Indicate all such expressions.
options: C. πd(r + h), where d = 2r is the diameter
D. πdh + πd²/2, where d = 2r is the diameter
questions.explanation: Total surface area = 2πr² (two bases) + 2πrh (lateral). A: 2πr(r + h) = 2πr² + 2πrh. B is the same. C: πd(r + h) = 2πr(r + h). D: πdh = 2πrh and πd²/2 = 2πr², so D is the same. E has only one base, πr², so it is wrong. Correct: A, B, C, D.
questions.trap: E counts only one circular base (the lateral area plus a single πr²).
questions.ets_note: Four near-identical equivalent forms; recall-style.

changes: replaced reordered duplicate D with a structurally different diameter form
Indicate-all-such wording

ets_rescore.prev_note: Four options are the same expression reworded; no real discrimination. Pure formula recall.

questions.question: A rectangular tank with a square base of side 6 m is filled with water to a depth of 4 m. How many cubic meters of water does the tank contain?
questions.explanation: The base is a 6 m × 6 m square. Volume of water = base area × depth = 6 × 6 × 4 = 144 m³.
questions.trap: Students compute 6 × 4 = 24 using only one side of the square base, forgetting the base is 6 m × 6 m, not 6 m wide. The square base contributes 6 × 6 = 36 m², giving 36 × 4 = 144 m³.

questions.question:
Sphere A has radius 3. Sphere B has radius 6.

Quantity A: Volume of Sphere B
Quantity B: 8 times the volume of Sphere A
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: V_A = (4/3)π(3³) = (4/3)π(27) = 36π. V_B = (4/3)π(6³) = (4/3)π(216) = 288π. Quantity B = 8 × 36π = 288π. The two quantities are equal. Since the radius doubled (k = 2), volume scales by k³ = 8.
questions.trap: Students think doubling the radius doubles the volume, expecting Quantity B = 2 × 36π = 72π < 288π, so they choose A. Volume scales by k³, not k. Doubling the radius → 2³ = 8 times the volume.

questions.question: A cylindrical water tank, open at the top, has radius 7 feet and height 10 feet. The entire outer surface of the tank, including the bottom, is to be painted. How many square feet will be painted? (Use π = 22/7.)
questions.explanation: An open-top cylinder has a lateral surface and a circular bottom (no top lid). Lateral SA = 2πrh = 2 × (22/7) × 7 × 10 = 2 × 22 × 10 = 440 sq ft. Circular bottom = πr² = (22/7) × 7² = (22/7) × 49 = 22 × 7 = 154 sq ft. Total = 440 + 154 = 594 sq ft.
questions.trap: Students include the top circle (closed cylinder), computing total SA = 2πr² + 2πrh = 308 + 440 = 748 sq ft. Since the tank is open at the top, only the bottom circle is included, not the top.
questions.ets_note: Open-top trap is good; 'use pi=22/7' is un-ETS-like.

questions.question: A cone has radius 6 cm and height 8 cm. What is its total surface area, in square centimeters?
questions.explanation: Slant height = √(6^2 + 8^2) = 10 cm. Lateral area = πrl = π(6)(10) = 60π. Base area = πr^2 = 36π. Total = 60π + 36π = 96π square centimeters. Answer: C.
questions.trap: A (60π) is the lateral area only, omitting the base. B (84π) uses the height 8 as the slant height: π(6)(8) + 36π. D (132π) counts the base twice: 60π + 36π + 36π. E (264π) treats the diameter 12 as the radius: π(12)(10) + π(12)^2.
