questions.question:
In the figure, A is the center of the circle and points B and D lie on the circle. Angle BAC is a right angle, C lies on ray AD beyond D, and DC is one-third the length of AD. The radius of the circle is 3m, where m is positive. Which of the following statements are true?

Indicate all such statements.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 271 240" width="271" height="240" role="img"><circle cx="119.8" cy="120" r="94" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4"/><line x1="119.8" y1="120" x2="119.8" y2="26" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="119.8" y1="120" x2="245.2" y2="120" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="119.8" y1="26" x2="245.2" y2="120" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><circle cx="119.8" cy="120" r="2.6" fill="#16191d" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><circle cx="119.8" cy="26" r="2.6" fill="#16191d" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><circle cx="213.8" cy="120" r="2.6" fill="#16191d" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><circle cx="245.2" cy="120" r="2.6" fill="#16191d" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M 119.8 112 L 127.8 112 L 127.8 120" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.1"/><text x="114.8" y="77.3" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">3m</text><text x="112.1" y="134.8" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">A</text><text x="118.1" y="17.6" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">B</text><text x="219.8" y="137.9" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">D</text><text x="254.2" y="124.7" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">C</text></svg>
options: A. The area of triangle ABC is 6*m^2.
B. The area of the sector bounded by radii AB and AD and the minor arc BD is 9*pi*m^2/4.
C. The area of that sector is greater than the area of triangle ABC.
D. The area of that sector is 9*pi*m^2.
E. The area of triangle ABC is greater than the area of that sector.
questions.explanation: Since AB and AD are radii, each has length 3m, and DC is one third of AD, so DC = m and AC = AD + DC = 4m. Triangle ABC has legs AB = 3m and AC = 4m meeting at the right angle at A, so its area is (1/2)(3m)(4m) = 6*m^2, which makes statement A true. The sector is a quarter of the circle because angle BAD is the same right angle, so its area is (1/4)(pi)(3m)^2 = 9*pi*m^2/4, which is about 7.07*m^2. That makes B true and D false. Comparing 7.07*m^2 with 6*m^2 shows the sector is the larger region, so C is true and E is false.
questions.trap: Students take the sector to be the whole circle and report 9*pi*m^2, or they treat AC as equal to AD and compute the triangle's area as 4.5*m^2, which would make the comparison look lopsided. The right angle at A makes the sector exactly one quarter of the circle, and C sits a third of a radius beyond D, so AC is four thirds of a radius.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Heavy statement count; mild textbook flavor.

questions.question:
Circle C and square S have the same perimeter. Which of the following statements must be true?

Indicate all such statements.
options: A. The area enclosed by C is greater than the area enclosed by S.
B. The ratio of the area enclosed by C to the area enclosed by S is 4/pi.
C. The area enclosed by C is more than 25 percent greater than the area enclosed by S.
D. The area enclosed by C is exactly twice the area enclosed by S.
E. The two enclosed areas are equal.
F. The ratio of the area enclosed by C to the area enclosed by S is pi/4.
questions.explanation: Call the common perimeter p. For the circle, 2*pi*r = p gives r = p/(2*pi), so its area is pi*r^2 = p^2/(4*pi). For the square, the side is p/4, so its area is p^2/16. Dividing, the ratio of circle area to square area is 16/(4*pi) = 4/pi, which is about 1.273. That makes B true and F false, since pi/4 is the reciprocal and is less than 1. A ratio above 1 makes A true, and 1.273 means the circle encloses about 27.3 percent more area, so C is true while D and E are false.
questions.trap: Students reach for pi/4, the familiar ratio of a circle's area to the area of the square that circumscribes it, and endorse F. That ratio applies when the square's side equals the circle's diameter, not when the two figures share a perimeter; with equal perimeters the circle is the larger region, so the ratio must exceed 1.

questions.question: Angle T measures t degrees. The complement of angle T measures 90 - t degrees and the supplement of angle T measures 180 - t degrees. If the measure of angle T is less than twice the measure of its complement and greater than one-third the measure of its supplement, which of the following gives all possible values of t?
questions.explanation: Turn each condition into an inequality. 'Less than twice its complement' gives t < 2(90 - t), so t < 180 - 2t, so 3t < 180 and t < 60. 'Greater than one-third its supplement' gives t > (180 - t)/3, so 3t > 180 - t, so 4t > 180 and t > 45. Both must hold at once, so 45 < t < 60.
questions.trap: Students solve only the first condition and pick 0 < t < 45 or 45 < t < 90, forgetting that the two conditions must be satisfied simultaneously. The lower bound 45 comes entirely from the supplement condition and the upper bound 60 entirely from the complement condition, so dropping either one widens the interval incorrectly.
questions.ets_note: Stem spells out complement and supplement expressions, handing over the setup; option B (30<t<45) is filler.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Stem restates complement/supplement definitions and is wordy; otherwise sound.

questions.question: An equilateral triangle has an altitude of length 9. What is the perimeter of the triangle?
questions.explanation: An altitude of an equilateral triangle splits it into two 30-60-90 triangles whose sides are in the ratio 1 : sqrt(3) : 2. The altitude is the sqrt(3) leg and the full side is the hypotenuse, so altitude = side * sqrt(3)/2. Setting side * sqrt(3)/2 = 9 gives side = 18/sqrt(3) = 6*sqrt(3). The perimeter is three times that: 18*sqrt(3).
questions.trap: Students treat the altitude as if it were a side and answer 27, or they correctly find the side 6*sqrt(3) and then forget to triple it, answering 6*sqrt(3). The altitude is always shorter than the side, so any answer at or below 9 per side is impossible.

questions.explanation: Work the two halves separately. Below the line, UH = 24 is a leg of two right triangles. In triangle VHU, VU = 25 and UH = 24, so VH = sqrt(625 - 576) = 7. In triangle AHU, UA = 26 and UH = 24, so HA = sqrt(676 - 576) = 10. Therefore VA = 7 + 10 = 17. Above the line, triangle VWB has a right angle at W and a 30-degree angle at B, so it is a 30-60-90 triangle in which VW is the side opposite the 30-degree angle. The hypotenuse VB is twice that side: VB = 2(25) = 50. Finally AB = VB - VA = 50 - 17 = 33.
questions.trap: Students find HA = 10 from the 10-24-26 triangle but forget that A is 7 units to the right of V, subtracting only 10 from 50 and answering 40. The point V sits 7 units left of H, so the whole segment VA is 17, not 10.

questions.question: The figure above shows a square with four interior line segments drawn in it. Each segment joins a vertex of the square to the midpoint of a side that does not contain that vertex, and the four segments bound the shaded quadrilateral in the middle. If the area of the square is 45, what is the area of the shaded quadrilateral?
questions.explanation: Put the square on a grid with side 1, corners at (0,0), (1,0), (1,1) and (0,1). The four segments are then the lines through (0,0) and (0.5,1), through (1,0) and (0,0.5), through (1,1) and (0.5,0), and through (0,1) and (1,0.5). Solving the four pairs of adjacent lines gives the corners of the middle quadrilateral, and its side turns out to be 1/sqrt(5) of the way across, so its area is 1/5 of the unit square. That fraction is the same for a square of any size, so the shaded area is 45/5 = 9.
questions.trap: Students eyeball the middle region as about a quarter of the square and answer 11.25. The four segments are steeper than the diagonals, which squeezes the middle region down to exactly one fifth, not one quarter.

questions.question:
Points P, Q and R lie on a line, with Q between P and R. Point S does not lie on that line. Ray QM bisects angle PQS and ray QN bisects angle SQR.
Quantity A: The measure, in degrees, of angle MQN
Quantity B: 90
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Because P, Q and R are collinear with Q in the middle, angles PQS and SQR are supplementary: their measures add to 180. Ray QM lies inside angle PQS and ray QN lies inside angle SQR, so angle MQN is made up of half of angle PQS plus half of angle SQR. That is (1/2)(angle PQS + angle SQR) = (1/2)(180) = 90 degrees, no matter where S sits.
questions.trap: Students see that neither angle PQS nor angle SQR is given a value and choose 'cannot be determined'. The individual angles really are unknown, but their sum is pinned at 180 by the straight line, and only the sum of the two halves is being asked for.

questions.question:
Polygon J has k sides, where k is greater than 4. Polygon K has k + 3 sides.
Quantity A: The sum of the measures of the interior angles of polygon K, in degrees
Quantity B: The sum of the measures of the interior angles of polygon J, in degrees, plus 480
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: The interior angles of an n-sided polygon sum to (n - 2)(180) degrees. Quantity A is therefore (k + 3 - 2)(180) = (k + 1)(180) = 180k + 180. Quantity B is (k - 2)(180) + 480 = 180k - 360 + 480 = 180k + 120. Subtracting, Quantity A minus Quantity B equals 60, a positive constant, so Quantity A is greater for every allowed k.
questions.trap: Students select 'cannot be determined' because k is unknown. The k terms cancel: adding three sides always adds exactly 3(180) = 540 degrees, and 540 is more than the 480 that Quantity B adds, so the gap is a fixed 60 degrees regardless of k.
questions.ets_note: One formula and short algebra; labelled hard but is medium. Condition k>4 is unused.

questions.question:
In the figure above, PQ = QR, point X lies on side PQ, point Y lies on side PR, and XY is perpendicular to PR. The area of triangle PXY is 1/8 the area of triangle PQR.

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
Quantity A: The length of PY
Quantity B: (1/8)(PR)
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 212" width="330" height="212" role="img"><polygon points="26,185.9 95.5,106 95.5,185.9" fill="#d8e1e9" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="0.01" stroke-linejoin="round"/><polygon points="26,185.9 165,26.1 304,185.9" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="95.5" y1="106" x2="95.5" y2="185.9" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M 103.5 185.9 L 103.5 177.9 L 95.5 177.9" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.1"/><text x="16.8" y="202.1" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">P</text><text x="313.2" y="202.1" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">R</text><text x="165" y="17.5" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">Q</text><text x="86.8" y="104.1" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">X</text><text x="95.5" y="204.9" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">Y</text></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Let M be the midpoint of PR. Since PQ = QR, the segment QM is the altitude from Q, so triangle PQM is a right triangle with legs PM = PR/2 and QM. Triangle PXY is similar to triangle PQM, because both have a right angle on PR and share the angle at P. If PY = k(PM), then the areas scale by k squared: area PXY = k^2 * area PQM. And area PQM is exactly half of area PQR. So area PXY = (k^2)/2 * area PQR. Setting (k^2)/2 = 1/8 gives k^2 = 1/4, so k = 1/2 and PY = (1/2)(PR/2) = PR/4. Since PR/4 is larger than PR/8, Quantity A is greater.
questions.trap: Students assume the area fraction transfers straight to the base and conclude PY = PR/8, choosing 'equal'. Shrinking a similar triangle by a factor k cuts its area by k squared, so an area of one eighth corresponds to a length factor of one half, not one eighth.

questions.question: All angles in the figure above are right angles, and the lengths of the six segments are as marked. What is the straight-line distance from point P to point Q?
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 249 200" width="249" height="200" role="img"><polyline points="25.8,174 99.8,174 99.8,124.7 149.2,124.7 149.2,50.7 223.2,50.7 223.2,26" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linejoin="round"/><circle cx="25.8" cy="174" r="2.6" fill="#16191d" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><circle cx="223.2" cy="26" r="2.6" fill="#16191d" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><text x="15.8" y="178.7" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">P</text><text x="228.2" y="19.2" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">Q</text><text x="62.8" y="194.3" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">3</text><text x="110.8" y="153.7" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">2</text><text x="124.5" y="115" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">2</text><text x="160.2" y="92" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">3</text><text x="186.2" y="41" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">3</text><text x="234.2" y="42.7" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">1</text></svg>
questions.explanation: Ignore the staircase shape and track only the net displacement. Moving from P to Q, the horizontal steps are 3, 2 and 3, for a total of 8 to the right. The vertical steps are 2, 3 and 1, for a total of 6 upward. The straight-line distance from P to Q is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with legs 8 and 6, which is a 6-8-10 triangle, so the distance is 10.
questions.trap: Students add all six segment lengths and answer 14, which is the length of the path walked, not the straight-line distance. The question asks for the direct segment PQ, so only the totals in each direction matter.

questions.question:
The figure above shows a park bounded by a right triangle whose horizontal side is 1,200 metres and whose vertical side is 900 metres. Five straight paths run through the park: the three vertical segments shown, the horizontal side, and the slanted side. The three vertical paths are parallel to one another, and the points where they meet the horizontal path are equally spaced 400 metres apart. If paving costs $84 per metre of path, what is the total cost, in dollars, of paving all five paths?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 207" width="320" height="207" role="img"><polygon points="26,180.8 232.2,180.8 232.2,26.2" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="94.7" y1="180.8" x2="94.7" y2="129.3" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="163.4" y1="180.8" x2="163.4" y2="77.7" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M 102.7 180.8 L 102.7 172.8 L 94.7 172.8" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.1"/><path d="M 171.4 180.8 L 171.4 172.8 L 163.4 172.8" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.1"/><path d="M 224.2 180.8 L 224.2 172.8 L 232.2 172.8" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.1"/><text x="129.1" y="202.1" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">1,200 metres</text><text x="242.2" y="107.8" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">900 metres</text></svg>
questions.explanation: The bounding right triangle has legs 1,200 and 900, so its hypotenuse is sqrt(1,200^2 + 900^2) = sqrt(1,440,000 + 810,000) = 1,500. The two interior vertical paths cut off triangles similar to the whole one. The first stands 400 metres along the base, so its height is 900(400/1200) = 300; the second stands 800 metres along, so its height is 900(800/1200) = 600. The five paths therefore measure 1,200 + 900 + 1,500 + 300 + 600 = 4,500 metres. At $84 per metre the cost is 4,500 x 84 = $378,000.
questions.trap: Students forget the hypotenuse, or they guess the interior heights as 450 and 600 by halving rather than by similarity. Each interior vertical is to 900 as its distance from the left corner is to 1,200, which gives 300 and 600, and the slanted path is a full 1,500 metres of paving.
questions.ets_note: Stem calls the 900 side one of the three verticals only via the figure; final 4500 x 84 multiplication is awkward.

ets_rescore.prev_note: 'Three vertical segments shown' never says one is the triangle's side; ambiguous.

questions.question: A rectangular garden has a perimeter of 84 metres, and its length and width are both integer numbers of metres. What is the difference between the greatest possible area and the least possible area, in square metres, of the garden?
questions.explanation: A perimeter of 84 means the length and width sum to 42. For a fixed sum, the product is largest when the two numbers are as close together as possible and smallest when they are as far apart as possible. The closest integer pair is 21 and 21, giving an area of 441. The farthest apart is 1 and 41, giving an area of 41. The difference is 441 - 41 = 400.
questions.trap: Students report 441 as the answer, stopping at the maximum, or they allow a side of 0 and claim a minimum area of 0, giving 441. A garden must have positive integer sides, so the thinnest allowed rectangle is 1 by 41, not 0 by 42.
questions.ets_note: Single-concept extreme-value check with one trap; labelled hard but is medium.

questions.question:
In triangle DEF, DE = 7 and EF = 16. Which of the following could be the perimeter of triangle DEF?

Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation: The third side DF must be greater than the difference of the two known sides and less than their sum: 16 - 7 = 9 and 16 + 7 = 23, so 9 < DF < 23. Adding the two known sides, the perimeter is DF + 23, which must satisfy 32 < perimeter < 46. Of the choices, 34, 38 and 44 fall strictly inside that interval. 30 is too small, and 46 and 52 are too large, with 46 excluded because the bound is strict.
questions.trap: Students include 46, forgetting that the inequality is strict. A third side of exactly 23 would make D, E and F collinear, which is not a triangle, so a perimeter of exactly 46 is impossible.

questions.question:
A rectangular photograph has a diagonal 25 centimetres long. One side of the photograph is longer than 7 centimetres and shorter than 15 centimetres. Which of the following could be the area, in square centimetres, of the photograph?

Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation: Call the given side s. The other side is sqrt(625 - s^2) and the area is s * sqrt(625 - s^2). At s = 7 the other side is sqrt(625 - 49) = 24, giving area 168. At s = 15 the other side is sqrt(625 - 225) = 20, giving area 300. The area of a rectangle with a fixed diagonal grows as the rectangle moves toward a square, and a square with diagonal 25 would have side about 17.7, so on the whole interval 7 < s < 15 the area is still increasing. The area therefore runs strictly between 168 and 300. Of the choices, 180, 240 and 294 qualify; 150 is below the range, and 300 and 320 are at or above it.
questions.trap: Students include 300, which is the value at exactly s = 15, an endpoint the problem excludes. Others cap the area at 312.5, the largest possible for a diagonal of 25, and wrongly admit 300 and even 320 on that basis; the side restriction pulls the ceiling down to 300 and makes it unreachable.

questions.question: J and K are two distinct points in a plane. Which of the following best describes the set of all points in that plane that are the same distance from J as they are from K?
options: A. The set contains no points
B. The set contains exactly one point
C. The set contains exactly two points
D. The set is a line
E. The set is a circle
questions.explanation: The midpoint of segment JK is one such point, so the set is not empty. Take any point M off the line JK with MJ = MK: triangle JMK is isosceles, and the perpendicular dropped from M to JK lands exactly on the midpoint. Conversely, every point on the line through the midpoint perpendicular to JK is equidistant from J and K, by the two congruent right triangles it creates. So the set is precisely the perpendicular bisector of JK, which is a line.
questions.trap: Students picture only the midpoint and answer 'exactly one point', or they think of 'equal distances from a point' and answer 'a circle'. A circle is the set of points a fixed distance from one centre; here the distances to two different points are being matched, and that produces a straight line.
questions.ets_note: Definition-level locus recall; labelled medium but is easy and textbook-flavoured.

questions.question: A rectangular hall floor is to be covered completely by square tiles whose sides are 6 inches long. The tiles are laid edge to edge with no gaps, and no tile is cut. If exactly 1,200 tiles are used, which of the following could be the dimensions of the floor? (Note: 12 inches = 1 foot.)
questions.explanation: A tile 6 inches on a side is half a foot on a side, so each tile covers (1/2)(1/2) = 0.25 square foot. Using 1,200 tiles covers 1,200 x 0.25 = 300 square feet. Checking the products: 12 x 20 = 240, 15 x 20 = 300, 15 x 25 = 375, 20 x 20 = 400, and 20 x 30 = 600. Only 15 feet by 20 feet gives 300 square feet, and both 15 and 20 are whole numbers of half-feet, so the tiles fit without cutting.
questions.trap: Students convert the side correctly to 0.5 foot but then use 0.5 square foot as the tile's area, doubling the total to 600 square feet and choosing 20 feet by 30 feet. Halving a length quarters the area, so the conversion factor is 0.25, not 0.5.

questions.question:
The parallel sides of trapezoid WXYZ have lengths XY = 5 and WZ = 13, and the nonparallel sides have lengths WX = 7 and YZ = 9, as shown above. Segment PQ (not shown) is parallel to the two parallel sides, with P on side WX and Q on side YZ. If PQ divides WXYZ into two trapezoids having equal perimeters, what is WP + QZ?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 195" width="330" height="195" role="img"><polygon points="26,169.2 68.8,25.8 175.7,25.8 304,169.2" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linejoin="round"/><text x="18.2" y="184" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">W</text><text x="61" y="20.4" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">X</text><text x="183.5" y="20.4" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">Y</text><text x="311.8" y="184" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">Z</text><text x="165" y="187.5" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">13</text><text x="122.2" y="16.1" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">5</text><text x="36.8" y="97.8" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">7</text><text x="248" y="92.5" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">9</text></svg>
questions.explanation: Let WP + QZ = p. Since P is on WX and Q is on YZ, the remaining pieces satisfy PX + YQ = (7 + 9) - p = 16 - p. The lower trapezoid WPQZ has perimeter WP + PQ + QZ + WZ = p + PQ + 13, and the upper trapezoid PXYQ has perimeter PX + XY + YQ + PQ = (16 - p) + 5 + PQ. Setting these equal, the shared PQ cancels: p + 13 = 21 - p, so 2p = 8 and p = 4.
questions.trap: Students split the nonparallel sides evenly, taking WP + QZ to be half of 7 + 9 = 16, and answer 8, or they halve the difference and answer 2. The cut is not a midline; it is placed so that the two 13-and-5 bases are balanced out, which pushes PQ well below the middle.

questions.question:
In the figure above, square JKLM is inscribed in rectangle ABCD so that J is the midpoint of AB and L is the midpoint of DC. Points P and Q are the midpoints of AD and BC, and K and M lie on segment PQ with PM = KQ = 6. If the area of square JKLM is 98, what is the area of rectangle ABCD?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 220" width="320" height="220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><rect x="30" y="35" width="260" height="140"/><line x1="30" y1="105" x2="290" y2="105" stroke-width="1"/><polygon points="160,35 230,105 160,175 90,105"/></g><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="18" y="30">A</text><text x="288" y="30">B</text><text x="288" y="192">C</text><text x="18" y="192">D</text><text x="156" y="28">J</text><text x="234" y="102">K</text><text x="156" y="192">L</text><text x="76" y="102">M</text><text x="16" y="118">P</text><text x="292" y="118">Q</text><text x="55" y="98">6</text><text x="253" y="98">6</text></g></svg>
questions.explanation: For a square, area equals half the square of a diagonal, so if the diagonals of JKLM have length d then d^2/2 = 98, giving d^2 = 196 and d = 14. Segment JL is one diagonal; since J and L are the midpoints of the opposite sides AB and DC, JL runs straight across the rectangle and equals the rectangle's height, so AD = 14. The other diagonal KM lies along PQ and also has length 14, so the rectangle's width is PM + MK + KQ = 6 + 14 + 6 = 26. The area is 14 x 26 = 364.
questions.trap: Students drop the two 6-unit pieces and answer 14 x 14 = 196, or they use the square's side 7*sqrt(2) as the rectangle's height. The rectangle's height is the square's diagonal, not its side, because J and L are opposite vertices of the square.

questions.question:
In the figure above, WXYZ is a rectangle and T is a point on side XY.

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
Quantity A: The area of triangular region WTZ
Quantity B: The sum of the areas of triangular regions WXT and TYZ
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 220" width="320" height="220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><rect x="40" y="50" width="230" height="130"/><line x1="40" y1="180" x2="150" y2="50"/><line x1="150" y1="50" x2="270" y2="180"/></g><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="26" y="196">W</text><text x="28" y="44">X</text><text x="272" y="44">Y</text><text x="272" y="196">Z</text><text x="146" y="42">T</text></g></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Let the rectangle have base WZ = b and height XW = h. Triangle WTZ has base WZ = b, and its apex T sits on the opposite side, so its height is the full h. Its area is (1/2)(b)(h), exactly half the rectangle's area bh. The two corner triangles WXT and TYZ together make up whatever is left of the rectangle, which is the other half. So the two quantities are equal, wherever T sits on XY.
questions.trap: Students try to compute the corner triangles separately, notice that T is not marked as a midpoint, and choose 'cannot be determined'. Sliding T along XY changes the two corner triangles individually but never changes their total, because the big triangle always claims exactly half the rectangle.

questions.question:
In the figure above, line BD is parallel to line AE, point B lies on segment AC, and point D lies on segment CE. Point F lies below line AE. The distance from C to line BD, marked y, equals the distance from F to line AE, marked x.

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
Quantity A: The area of triangular region ACE
Quantity B: The area of triangular region BDF
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 177" width="320" height="177" role="img"><polygon points="26,115.3 160,26 294,115.3" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="106.4" y1="61.7" x2="213.6" y2="61.7" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="106.4" y1="61.7" x2="160" y2="151" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="213.6" y1="61.7" x2="160" y2="151" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="160" y1="26" x2="160" y2="61.7" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="160" y1="151" x2="160" y2="115.3" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><path d="M 167 61.7 L 167 54.7 L 160 54.7" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.1"/><path d="M 167 115.3 L 167 122.3 L 160 122.3" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.1"/><text x="155" y="48.2" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end" font-style="italic">y</text><text x="156" y="133.2" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end" font-style="italic">x</text><text x="16.6" y="124.5" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">A</text><text x="303.4" y="124.5" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">E</text><text x="160" y="17.4" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="97.7" y="59.8" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">B</text><text x="222.3" y="59.8" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">D</text><text x="160" y="169" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">F</text></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Let d be the distance between the two parallel lines BD and AE. The height of triangle ACE, measured from C down to base AE, is y + d. The height of triangle BDF, measured from F up to base BD, is x + d. Since x = y, those two heights are equal, so the areas are decided entirely by the bases. Now BD is a segment cut across triangle ACE parallel to AE with B on AC and D on CE, so BD is strictly shorter than AE. A larger base with the same height gives a larger area, so triangle ACE is greater.
questions.trap: Students compare only x with y, see that they are equal, and choose 'equal'. The two triangles do share a common height, but their bases differ: BD is a shortened copy of AE produced by the parallel cut, so equal heights leave ACE strictly bigger.

questions.question:
Line segment AD has length 40. Point B lies on AD, and segment BD has length 22. Point C also lies on AD, and segment BC has length 5.
Quantity A: The length of AC
Quantity B: The length of AB
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Since B is on AD with BD = 22, we get AB = 40 - 22 = 18, so Quantity B is fixed at 18. But C is only pinned down as a point of AD that is 5 units from B, and there are two such points: one 5 units toward A, giving AC = 13, and one 5 units toward D, giving AC = 23. Both lie within the segment, since 13 and 23 are both between 0 and 40. So Quantity A can be less than 18 or greater than 18, and the relationship cannot be determined.
questions.trap: Students place C automatically on the far side of B, compute AC = 23, and answer that Quantity A is greater. Saying that C is on the segment and 5 units from B leaves two legitimate positions, and the two give opposite comparisons.

questions.question: What is the ratio of the area of a square region with diagonal 6 to the area of a square region with diagonal 15? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.explanation: A square with diagonal d has side d/sqrt(2), so its area is d^2/2. The first square has area 36/2 = 18 and the second has area 225/2 = 112.5. The ratio is 18/112.5 = 4/25. More directly, area scales as the square of any single length measurement, so the ratio of areas is (6/15)^2 = (2/5)^2 = 4/25.
questions.trap: Students report 6/15 = 2/5, giving the ratio of the diagonals rather than the ratio of the areas. Areas of similar figures scale as the square of the length ratio, so the 2/5 must be squared.

questions.question: A boat builder is cutting two sails, each in the shape of a right triangle whose legs are a vertical edge and a horizontal edge. Sail A has a vertical edge of length 24 feet and a hypotenuse of length 26 feet. Sail B has a vertical edge of length 20 feet and a hypotenuse of length 20.5 feet. How many square feet greater is the area of sail A than the area of sail B?
questions.explanation: For sail A the horizontal edge is sqrt(26^2 - 24^2) = sqrt(676 - 576) = sqrt(100) = 10, so its area is (1/2)(24)(10) = 120 square feet. For sail B the horizontal edge is sqrt(20.5^2 - 20^2) = sqrt(420.25 - 400) = sqrt(20.25) = 4.5, so its area is (1/2)(20)(4.5) = 45 square feet. The difference is 120 - 45 = 75 square feet.
questions.trap: Students take the hypotenuse as the second leg and compute areas of (1/2)(24)(26) = 312 and (1/2)(20)(20.5) = 205, reporting 107. In a right triangle only the two legs multiply to twice the area; the hypotenuse must first be converted into the missing leg by the Pythagorean theorem.
questions.ets_note: Sail B (hypotenuse 20.5, leg 4.5) forces decimal squaring; scaled 9-40-41 triple is not GRE-clean.

ets_difficulty_recal.work_required: Two right triangles solved by Pythagoras and areas subtracted; one concept repeated.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Two Pythagorean calculations, fine; stem needs unit/figure-free phrasing but hard label overstated.

questions.question:
A plank 26 feet long rests horizontally on a support placed at the plank's midpoint, and the top of the support is 5 feet above level ground, as shown above. The plank is then tilted about the support, which stays at the plank's midpoint, until the left end of the plank just touches the ground. How many feet above the ground is the right end of the plank at that moment?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 142" width="330" height="142" role="img"><line x1="26" y1="115.8" x2="304" y2="115.8" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><polygon points="148.9,115.8 172.2,115.8 160.5,71" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="43.9" y1="71" x2="277.1" y2="71" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="2.0" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="52.9" y1="115.8" x2="268.1" y2="26.2" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><line x1="268.1" y1="115.8" x2="268.1" y2="26.2" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.0" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/><circle cx="160.5" cy="71" r="2.4" fill="#16191d" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><path d="M 275.1 115.8 L 275.1 108.8 L 268.1 108.8" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.1"/><text x="102.2" y="65.3" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">26 ft</text><text x="171.9" y="98.6" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">5 ft</text><text x="274.1" y="52" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">?</text><text x="304" y="133.8" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="11" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">ground</text></svg>
questions.explanation: The support touches the plank at its midpoint, so each half of the plank is 13 feet long. Look at the left half: it runs from the support, 5 feet above the ground, down to the ground, so it is the hypotenuse of a right triangle with vertical leg 5 and hypotenuse 13 (a 5-12-13 triangle). The right half is the same 13-foot length tilted by the same angle in the opposite direction, so its far end rises 5 feet above the support. The support is already 5 feet up, so the right end is 5 + 5 = 10 feet above the ground.
questions.trap: Students answer 5, reading off only the height gained above the support, or they answer 13 by treating the half-plank as vertical. The two halves are mirror images about the support, so the right end climbs as far above the support as the left end dropped below it, and the support's own 5 feet must be added on.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Stem says plank starts horizontal but figure already shows tilted plank touching ground; minor mismatch.

questions.question:
A surveyor measures the distance from a marker M to post P as 18 metres and the distance from M to post Q as 11 metres. The three points are not in a straight line. Which of the following could be the distance, in metres, between P and Q?

Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation: Because M, P and Q form a genuine triangle, the side PQ must be greater than the difference of the other two sides and less than their sum: 18 - 11 = 7 and 18 + 11 = 29, so 7 < PQ < 29. Of the choices, 12, 20 and 28 lie strictly inside that range. 5 is too small, 7 is the excluded lower bound, and 31 exceeds the upper bound.
questions.trap: Students admit 7, forgetting that a distance of exactly 7 would put all three points on one line, which the problem rules out. The two bounds 7 and 29 are the collinear cases and are never attainable for a real triangle.

questions.question:
A cycling route runs in a straight line from a trailhead to a lookout 62.5 kilometres away. A water station stands on the route 47.2 kilometres from the trailhead, and a ranger is always within 0.8 kilometre of the water station, measured along the route. A cyclist's bicycle broke down on the route at a point less than 0.6 kilometre before the lookout. Which of the following could be the distance, in kilometres, along the route between the bicycle and the ranger?

Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation: Measure everything from the trailhead. The bicycle sits strictly between 62.5 - 0.6 = 61.9 and 62.5, since 'less than 0.6 kilometre before the lookout' excludes both endpoints. The ranger sits somewhere from 47.2 - 0.8 = 46.4 to 47.2 + 0.8 = 48.0. The gap between them is smallest when the bicycle is as far back as possible and the ranger as far forward as possible: 61.9 - 48.0 = 13.9. It is largest when the bicycle is as far forward as possible and the ranger as far back as possible: 62.5 - 46.4 = 16.1. Both extremes come from the bicycle's excluded endpoints, so the distance runs strictly between 13.9 and 16.1. Only 14.0, 14.8 and 15.6 qualify.
questions.trap: Students take 16.1 because it looks like the stated maximum. Reaching 16.1 would require the bicycle to be exactly at the lookout, which the phrase 'less than 0.6 kilometre before the lookout' forbids, so the top of the range is open. Others compute the centre gap 62.5 - 47.2 = 15.3 and spread it only by 0.8, missing the 0.6 from the bicycle's own uncertainty.
questions.ets_note: Decimal-heavy interval bookkeeping; 16.1 hinges on reading 'less than 0.6 km before the lookout' as excluding the lookout.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Decimal-heavy cover story; answer hinges on strict vs inclusive endpoints rather than insight.

questions.question: A town ordinance requires that a room used for an indoor gathering provide at least 24 square feet of floor space for every 3 people attending. A gathering is to be held in a rectangular hall whose floor measures 36 feet by 60 feet. According to the ordinance, what is the greatest number of people permitted to attend?
questions.explanation: The floor area is 36 x 60 = 2,160 square feet. The ordinance allots 24 square feet to every group of 3 people, so the hall supports 2,160/24 = 90 such groups. Each group is 3 people, so the maximum attendance is 90 x 3 = 270. Equivalently, the rule is 8 square feet per person, and 2,160/8 = 270.
questions.trap: Students divide 2,160 by 24 and stop, answering 90. That count is the number of 3-person groups, not the number of people, so it must still be tripled. Dividing by 3 instead of multiplying gives 30, which is far too small to appear as a trap but reflects the same slip.

questions.question: A regular hexagon is inscribed in a circle whose diameter is 18. What is the perimeter of the hexagon?
questions.explanation: Join the centre of the circle to each of the six vertices. This splits the hexagon into six triangles, each with two sides equal to the radius and a central angle of 360/6 = 60 degrees. A triangle with two equal sides and a 60-degree angle between them is equilateral, so each side of the hexagon equals the radius. The diameter is 18, so the radius and therefore each side is 9, and the perimeter is 6 x 9 = 54.
questions.trap: Students set the side equal to the diameter and answer 108, or they bring in a sqrt(3) from the equilateral triangle's altitude and answer 54*sqrt(3). The equilateral triangles here give side = radius exactly, with no radical involved; the sqrt(3) belongs to the hexagon's height, not its side.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 240 240" width="240" height="240" role="img"><circle cx="120" cy="120" r="94" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4"/><polygon points="214,120 167,38.6 73,38.6 26,120 73,201.4 167,201.4" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="26" y1="120" x2="214" y2="120" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><text x="120" y="114.3" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">18</text></svg>

ets_rescore.prev_note: Fine standard item.

questions.question: The advertised size of a television is the length of the diagonal of its rectangular viewing screen. For a television advertised as 55-inch, if the lengths of the sides of the viewing screen are in the ratio 16 to 9, which of the following is closest to the area, in square inches, of the viewing screen?
questions.explanation: Write the sides as 16x and 9x. By the Pythagorean theorem the diagonal is x*sqrt(16^2 + 9^2) = x*sqrt(256 + 81) = x*sqrt(337). Setting x*sqrt(337) = 55 gives x^2 = 55^2/337 = 3,025/337, which is about 8.98. The area is (16x)(9x) = 144x^2, which is about 144 x 8.98 = 1,293 square inches.
questions.trap: Students treat 16, 9 and the diagonal as a 16-9-25 triple, set x = 55/25 = 2.2, and compute 144(2.2)^2 = 697. The hypotenuse of a 16-9 right triangle is sqrt(337), roughly 18.36, not 25, so the scale factor is close to 3, not 2.2.
questions.ets_note: Requires dividing by 337 and multiplying by 144 with no simplifying insight; calculator work.

questions.question:
The figure above is a scale drawing of the floor of a workshop in which all the walls meet at right angles. The measurements shown on the drawing, including the two sides of length x, are in centimetres, and the drawing uses a scale of 1 centimetre to 2 metres. If the perimeter of the drawing is 45.2 centimetres, approximately what is the area, in square metres, of the workshop floor?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 160" width="320" height="160" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><polyline points="40,130 263,130 263,35 175,35 175,75 75,75 75,35 40,35 40,130"/></g><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="138" y="148">12.4</text><text x="114" y="94">3.5</text><text x="181" y="59">1.6</text><text x="26" y="87">x</text><text x="270" y="87">x</text></g></svg>
questions.explanation: Trace the perimeter. The bottom is 12.4 and the two vertical sides are each x. Along the top, the two flat pieces plus the notch's own floor still add up to 12.4 horizontally, and the notch contributes two extra vertical pieces of 1.6 each. So the perimeter is 12.4 + 2x + 12.4 + 2(1.6) = 28 + 2x. Setting 28 + 2x = 45.2 gives x = 8.6. The area on the drawing is the full rectangle minus the notch: 12.4 x 8.6 - 3.5 x 1.6 = 106.64 - 5.6 = 101.04 square centimetres. Since 1 centimetre represents 2 metres, 1 square centimetre represents 4 square metres, so the floor is 101.04 x 4 = 404.16, or about 404 square metres.
questions.trap: Students scale the area by 2 instead of by 4 and answer 202, or they forget to subtract the notch and answer about 427. A linear scale factor of 2 becomes a factor of 2 squared when areas are converted, and the notch really is missing from the floor.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Ugly decimals; 427 filler distractor.

questions.question:
A hexagon has six interior angles. Five of those angles each measure 128 degrees.
Quantity A: The measure, in degrees, of the sixth interior angle
Quantity B: 128
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: The interior angles of an n-sided polygon sum to (n - 2)(180) degrees, so for a hexagon the total is (6 - 2)(180) = 720. The five given angles account for 5 x 128 = 640 degrees, leaving 720 - 640 = 80 degrees for the sixth. Since 80 is less than 128, Quantity B is greater.
questions.trap: Students recall that a regular hexagon has 120-degree angles, notice that 128 exceeds 120, and conclude the remaining angle must also be large, choosing A. Five angles pushed above the regular value force the sixth well below it, because the total is locked at 720.

questions.question:
In the figure above, EFGH is a convex quadrilateral and EG and FH are its diagonals.

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
Quantity A: The perimeter of EFGH
Quantity B: EG + FH
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 220" width="320" height="220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><polygon points="50,60 160,25 275,110 140,195"/><line x1="50" y1="60" x2="275" y2="110"/><line x1="160" y1="25" x2="140" y2="195"/></g><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="34" y="56">E</text><text x="158" y="18">F</text><text x="281" y="108">G</text><text x="136" y="212">H</text></g></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Each diagonal splits the quadrilateral into two triangles, and in every triangle the sum of two sides exceeds the third. Using diagonal EG: EF + FG > EG and GH + HE > EG. Using diagonal FH: EF + HE > FH and FG + GH > FH. Adding all four inequalities, the left side gives 2(EF + FG + GH + HE), which is twice the perimeter, and the right side gives 2(EG + FH). Dividing by 2 shows the perimeter is greater than EG + FH, for every convex quadrilateral.
questions.trap: Students test one square, find perimeter 4s against diagonals 2s*sqrt(2) which is about 2.83s, then worry that a long thin quadrilateral could reverse it and pick D. Stretching the shape stretches the sides at least as fast as the diagonals; the four triangle inequalities hold in every case, so the ordering never flips.

questions.question:
In the figure above, angle B of triangle ABC is a right angle and AB = BC. Square DEFG is inscribed in the triangle, with D and G on side AC, E on side AB, and F on side BC.

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
Quantity A: The area of triangular region ADE
Quantity B: (1/4) of the area of triangular region ABC
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 220" width="320" height="220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="28,180 116,180 116,92" fill="#e5edf7" stroke="none"/><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><polygon points="28,180 292,180 160,48"/><rect x="116" y="92" width="88" height="88"/><polyline points="150,58 160,68 170,58"/></g><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="16" y="194">A</text><text x="155" y="40">B</text><text x="296" y="194">C</text><text x="109" y="196">D</text><text x="98" y="88">E</text><text x="208" y="88">F</text><text x="199" y="196">G</text></g></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Let the hypotenuse AC have length a. Since AB = BC and angle B is 90 degrees, angles A and C each measure 45 degrees, and the altitude from B to AC is a/2. Let the square have side s. Because angle A is 45 degrees and ED is perpendicular to AC, triangle ADE is an isosceles right triangle, so AD = ED = s. By the same argument at C, GC = s. Then AC = AD + DG + GC = s + s + s = 3s, so s = a/3. The area of ADE is (1/2)(a/3)(a/3) = a^2/18. The area of ABC is (1/2)(a)(a/2) = a^2/4, so Quantity B is (1/4)(a^2/4) = a^2/16. Since a^2/16 is larger than a^2/18, Quantity B is greater.
questions.trap: Students assume the inscribed square sits symmetrically enough that the corner triangle is a clean quarter of the whole and choose 'equal'. The square's side is a full third of the hypotenuse, which makes each corner triangle 2/9 of the big triangle, slightly less than a quarter.

questions.question: A farm is made up of two fields whose areas are 2.5 acres and 1.5 acres. What is the total area, in square feet, of the two fields combined? (Note: 1 acre = 4,840 square yards, and 1 yard = 3 feet.)
questions.explanation: The two fields total 2.5 + 1.5 = 4 acres. In square yards that is 4 x 4,840 = 19,360. Since 1 yard is 3 feet, 1 square yard is 3 x 3 = 9 square feet, so the total in square feet is 19,360 x 9 = 174,240.
questions.trap: Students multiply by 3 rather than 9 when converting square yards to square feet and answer 58,080. A length conversion factor of 3 becomes 3 squared when areas are converted.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Acre conversions outside ETS style; large unwieldy numbers.

questions.question: The figure above shows a square tile 20 centimetres on a side. In the centre of the tile is a square region 15 centimetres on a side, divided into nine congruent smaller squares. Five of those nine smaller squares are grey, as shown, and the rest of the tile is white. What fraction of the area of the tile is grey? Give your answer as a fraction.
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 280 280" width="280" height="280" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g fill="#e5edf7" stroke="none"><rect x="55" y="45" width="50" height="50"/><rect x="155" y="45" width="50" height="50"/><rect x="105" y="95" width="50" height="50"/><rect x="55" y="145" width="50" height="50"/><rect x="155" y="145" width="50" height="50"/></g><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><rect x="30" y="20" width="200" height="200"/><rect x="55" y="45" width="150" height="150"/><line x1="105" y1="45" x2="105" y2="195"/><line x1="155" y1="45" x2="155" y2="195"/><line x1="55" y1="95" x2="205" y2="95"/><line x1="55" y1="145" x2="205" y2="145"/></g><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="96" y="242">20 cm</text><text x="98" y="214">15 cm</text></g></svg>
questions.explanation: Work in two steps. First, the inner square compared with the whole tile: their sides are 15 and 20, and areas scale as the square of the side ratio, so the inner square is (15/20)^2 = (3/4)^2 = 9/16 of the tile. Second, the grey part of the inner square: 5 of the 9 congruent small squares are grey, so that is 5/9 of the inner square. The grey share of the whole tile is therefore (5/9)(9/16) = 5/16.
questions.trap: Students report 5/9, the grey fraction of the inner square only, or they scale by 15/20 instead of its square and get (5/9)(3/4) = 5/12. The inner square covers only 9/16 of the tile, not 3/4 of it, because the 3/4 applies to lengths.
questions.ets_note: Short area count; labelled hard but is easy to medium.

questions.question:
A triangle is drawn inside a rectangle so that one side of the triangle is an entire side of the rectangle and the opposite vertex of the triangle lies on the opposite side of the rectangle. The rectangle has perimeter 28, and its length and width are both integers. Which of the following could be the area of the triangle?

Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation: A perimeter of 28 means the length and width sum to 14. The triangle has base equal to one side of the rectangle and height equal to the other side, so its area is half the rectangle's area. Running through the integer pairs whose sum is 14 gives areas of (1)(13)/2 = 6.5, (2)(12)/2 = 12, (3)(11)/2 = 16.5, (4)(10)/2 = 20, (5)(9)/2 = 22.5, (6)(8)/2 = 24 and (7)(7)/2 = 24.5. Of the choices, 6.5, 16.5 and 20 appear on that list; 10, 26 and 28 do not.
questions.trap: Students forget the halving and look for products of integer pairs summing to 14, picking 28 (which would be 2 x 12 halved wrongly) or 26. The triangle is always exactly half the rectangle, and the largest possible value is 24.5, so anything above that is impossible.

questions.question:
On a map drawn to scale, the point marking town A is 6 inches from the point marking town B, and the point marking town B is 2.5 inches from the point marking town C. The actual distance from town A to town B is 210 kilometres, and the three towns are not in a straight line. Which of the following could be the actual distance, in kilometres, from town A to town C?

Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation: First fix the scale: 6 inches represents 210 kilometres, so 1 inch represents 35 kilometres. Then town B to town C is 2.5 x 35 = 87.5 kilometres. Since the three towns form a genuine triangle, AC must lie strictly between the difference and the sum of the other two sides: 210 - 87.5 = 122.5 and 210 + 87.5 = 297.5, so 122.5 < AC < 297.5. Of the choices, 140, 210 and 280 fall inside. 105 is below the range, 350 is above it, and 297.5 is the excluded upper bound.
questions.trap: Students select 297.5, the exact sum of the two sides, which would place the three towns on one line and is ruled out by the problem. Others skip the scale conversion and use 2.5 kilometres for BC, producing the far narrower range 207.5 to 212.5 and admitting only 210.

questions.question: A gallery wall is covered by 48 flat rectangular panels. If each panel measures 5 feet by 4.5 feet, what is the total area, in square yards, of the panels? (Note: 1 yard = 3 feet.)
questions.explanation: Each panel covers 5 x 4.5 = 22.5 square feet, so 48 panels cover 48 x 22.5 = 1,080 square feet. Since 1 yard is 3 feet, 1 square yard is 3 x 3 = 9 square feet. Converting, 1,080/9 = 120 square yards.
questions.trap: Students divide the square-foot total by 3 instead of 9 and answer 360, or they leave the answer in square feet and choose 1,080. Converting an area between feet and yards uses the square of the length factor, so the divisor is 9.

questions.question: The figure above represents a marsh and the dry land around it. A surveyor needs the distance from point A to point B, which lie on opposite edges of the marsh and cannot be measured directly. She chooses a point R on dry land, extends line AR beyond R to a point D, and extends line BR beyond R to a point C, placing C and D so that segment CD is parallel to segment AB. She then measures RD and DC. Of the following, which additional measurement would be sufficient to determine the distance from A to B?
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 320 198" width="320" height="198" role="img"><polygon points="253.9,31.2 294,76.4 289,131.6 233.8,166.8 153.5,171.8 123.4,146.7 98.3,106.5 133.4,61.4 193.6,26.2" fill="#d8e1e9" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="253.9" y1="31.2" x2="123.4" y2="146.7" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="253.9" y1="31.2" x2="26" y2="77.4" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="123.4" y1="146.7" x2="65.1" y2="42.3" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="65.1" y1="42.3" x2="26" y2="77.4" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><circle cx="253.9" cy="31.2" r="2.6" fill="#16191d" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><circle cx="123.4" cy="146.7" r="2.6" fill="#16191d" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><circle cx="65.1" cy="42.3" r="2.6" fill="#16191d" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><circle cx="26" cy="77.4" r="2.6" fill="#16191d" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><circle cx="78.8" cy="66.7" r="2.6" fill="#16191d" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1"/><text x="260.9" y="26.6" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">A</text><text x="116.3" y="160.7" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">B</text><text x="61.7" y="34.5" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">C</text><text x="16.6" y="86.6" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">D</text><text x="74.7" y="85.7" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">R</text></svg>
options: A. The distance from A to R
B. The distance from B to R
C. The distance from C to R
D. The measure of angle ARB
E. The measure of angle RAB
questions.explanation: Because CD is parallel to AB, the transversals give equal alternate interior angles, and angles DRC and ARB are vertical angles, so triangle RDC is similar to triangle RAB. Corresponding sides are then in proportion: RD/RA = DC/AB, which rearranges to AB = DC(RA)/RD. The surveyor already has DC and RD, so the one missing piece is RA, the distance from A to R. Knowing BR or CR instead would give the other proportion RC/RB = DC/AB, in which two of the three needed lengths would still be unknown, and an angle alone never fixes a length.
questions.trap: Students pick the measure of angle ARB, reasoning that an angle plus two sides determines a triangle. Angle ARB is already equal to angle DRC and so adds nothing new; similarity has already been established, and what is missing is the scale factor, which only a length along the same pair of corresponding sides can supply.

questions.question:
In triangle JKL above, the three angle bisectors meet at point N. If angle NLJ measures 21 degrees and angle NJL measures 34 degrees, what is the measure, in degrees, of angle JKN?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 236" width="330" height="236" role="img"><polygon points="26,209.8 100.2,26.2 304,209.8" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="26" y1="209.8" x2="126.8" y2="141.8" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="100.2" y1="26.2" x2="126.8" y2="141.8" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="304" y1="209.8" x2="126.8" y2="141.8" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M 54.2 190.8 A 34 34 0 0 1 60 209.8" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.1"/><path d="M 264 209.8 A 40 40 0 0 1 266.7 195.4" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.1"/><text x="72.9" y="198.6" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="11" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">34°</text><text x="249.9" y="203.2" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="11" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">21°</text><text x="16.8" y="225.9" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">J</text><text x="313.2" y="225.9" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">L</text><text x="100.2" y="17.7" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">K</text><text x="128.1" y="160.6" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">N</text></svg>
questions.explanation: Since JN bisects angle J, the full angle J is 2(34) = 68 degrees. Since LN bisects angle L, the full angle L is 2(21) = 42 degrees. The three angles of triangle JKL sum to 180, so angle K = 180 - 68 - 42 = 70 degrees. KN bisects angle K, so angle JKN is half of that: 35 degrees.
questions.trap: Students find angle K = 70 and stop, choosing 70 without halving it for the bisector. Others forget to double the two given half-angles, computing 180 - 34 - 21 = 125 and then halving to 62.5. The two given angles are halves and the answer is a half, so both doublings and one halving are needed.
questions.ets_note: Double, subtract, halve; labelled hard but is easy to medium.

questions.question: The lengths of the sides of a triangle are 5, 12 and w. Which of the following inequalities specifies exactly those values of w for which every angle of the triangle measures less than 90 degrees?
questions.explanation: The angle opposite the longest side is the largest angle, and comparing the square of the longest side with the sum of the squares of the other two decides whether it is acute, right or obtuse. If w is the longest side, acuteness requires w^2 < 5^2 + 12^2 = 169, so w < 13. If 12 is the longest side, acuteness requires 12^2 < 5^2 + w^2, that is 144 < 25 + w^2, so w^2 > 119 and w > sqrt(119). Since sqrt(119) is about 10.9, which already exceeds the triangle-inequality floor of 7, the binding conditions are sqrt(119) < w < 13.
questions.trap: Students apply only the triangle inequality, 12 - 5 = 7 and 12 + 5 = 17, and pick 7 < w < 17. That range merely guarantees a triangle exists; it happily includes w = 8, where 12 is long enough to sit opposite an obtuse angle since 144 exceeds 25 + 64.

questions.question:
ABCD is a square, and AC is one of its diagonals.
Quantity A: (AB + BC)/AC
Quantity B: 1.5
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Let the side of the square be s. Then AB = BC = s, and AC is a diagonal, which for a square equals s*sqrt(2). Quantity A is therefore (s + s)/(s*sqrt(2)) = 2s/(s*sqrt(2)) = 2/sqrt(2) = sqrt(2). Since sqrt(2) is about 1.414, which is less than 1.5, Quantity B is greater. The side length cancels, so this holds for every square.
questions.trap: Students reason that going along two sides must be much longer than cutting across, and guess a ratio near 2, choosing A. The diagonal is already sqrt(2) times a side, so two sides compared with one diagonal gives only 2/sqrt(2) = sqrt(2), which falls just short of 1.5.

questions.question:
In quadrilateral KLMN above, side LM is parallel to side KN, LM is shorter than KN, and angle K is a right angle.

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
Quantity A: The length of KL
Quantity B: The length of MN
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 220" width="320" height="220" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><polygon points="50,190 50,60 170,60 270,190"/><polyline points="50,178 62,178 62,190"/></g><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="36" y="206">K</text><text x="36" y="56">L</text><text x="172" y="52">M</text><text x="276" y="206">N</text></g></svg>
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Because angle K is a right angle and LM is parallel to KN, side KL is perpendicular to both parallel lines, so KL is exactly the perpendicular distance between them. Now drop a perpendicular from M to line KN, meeting it at a point F. Then MF also equals that same distance, so MF = KL. Since LM is shorter than KN, the point F falls strictly between K and N, so FN is a positive length and triangle MFN is a genuine right triangle with legs MF and FN and hypotenuse MN. A hypotenuse always exceeds either leg, so MN is greater than MF = KL.
questions.trap: Students see no numbers and choose 'cannot be determined'. The perpendicular side KL is the shortest possible segment between the two parallel lines, and because LM is strictly shorter than KN the side MN must slant, which forces it to be strictly longer, whatever the actual measurements are.

questions.question:
O is a point in a plane, and X, Y and Z are three distinct points in that same plane with OX = OY = OZ = 9.
Quantity A: XY
Quantity B: YZ
options: C. The two quantities are equal.
D. The relationship cannot be determined from the information given.
questions.explanation: Saying that X, Y and Z are all 9 units from O places all three on one circle of radius 9 centred at O, but it says nothing about where on that circle they sit. The length XY depends only on the central angle XOY, and YZ only on the central angle YOZ, and those two angles are completely free. For instance, putting X, Y and Z at 0, 60 and 180 degrees around the circle makes XY = 9 and YZ = 9*sqrt(3), so Quantity B wins; swapping the roles of X and Z makes Quantity A win. Nothing decides between them.
questions.trap: Students read three equal distances from one point as forcing an equilateral triangle and answer 'equal'. Equal distances from O only put the three points on a common circle; the chords between them still vary with how the points are spaced around it.
questions.ets_note: Two quick cases settle it; labelled hard but is easy to medium.

questions.question:
In triangle ABC above, angle A is a right angle, AB = 20 and AC = 48. Point D lies on side AC with AD = (5/12)(AC). What is the measure, in degrees, of angle BDC?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 330 205" width="330" height="205" role="img"><polygon points="26,141.6 26,25.8 304,141.6" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linejoin="round"/><line x1="26" y1="25.8" x2="141.8" y2="141.6" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="26" y1="173.4" x2="304" y2="173.4" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.0" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="26" y1="179.2" x2="26" y2="167.7" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.0" stroke-linecap="round"/><line x1="304" y1="179.2" x2="304" y2="167.7" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.0" stroke-linecap="round"/><path d="M 36 141.6 L 36 131.6 L 26 131.6" fill="none" stroke="#16191d" stroke-width="1.1"/><text x="15" y="88" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">20</text><text x="165" y="191.8" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="12" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">48</text><text x="13.8" y="151.8" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">A</text><text x="16.8" y="18.9" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="end">B</text><text x="316.2" y="151.8" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="start">C</text><text x="141.8" y="160.5" font-family="Georgia,serif" font-size="13" fill="#16191d" text-anchor="middle">D</text></svg>
questions.explanation: First locate D: AD = (5/12)(48) = 20. So in triangle ABD the two legs at the right angle A are AB = 20 and AD = 20, making it an isosceles right triangle. Its two acute angles are therefore 45 degrees each, so angle ADB = 45. Since D lies on segment AC, angles ADB and BDC together form a straight angle, so angle BDC = 180 - 45 = 135 degrees.
questions.trap: Students compute angle ADB = 45 and submit that, answering the wrong angle. Angle BDC is the one on the far side of D, the supplement of angle ADB, so it is obtuse at 135 degrees.

questions.question: A 25-foot ladder leans against a vertical wall with the base of the ladder 7 feet from the wall. The base is then pulled 8 feet farther from the wall, and the top of the ladder slides down the wall. By how many feet does the top of the ladder drop?
questions.explanation: The ladder, the wall and the ground form a right triangle with the ladder as the 25-foot hypotenuse. At first the base is 7 feet out, so the top reaches sqrt(625 - 49) = sqrt(576) = 24 feet up the wall. After the base is pulled out 8 more feet it sits 15 feet from the wall, so the top now reaches sqrt(625 - 225) = sqrt(400) = 20 feet. The top therefore drops 24 - 20 = 4 feet.
questions.trap: Students assume the top falls as far as the base moves and answer 8. The two distances are linked by the Pythagorean theorem, not by a one-to-one trade: near the vertical position the top barely moves, so an 8-foot pull out costs only 4 feet of height here.

questions.ets_note: Two applications of 7-24-25 and 15-20-25 triples; labelled hard but is medium.

questions.question:
In the figure above, ACEG is a square. Square ABIH shares vertex A with it, with B on side AC and H on side AG. Square JDEF shares vertex E with it, with D on side CE and F on side EG. Squares ABIH and JDEF have equal areas, and the area of square ACEG is 25 times the area of square ABIH. BJFI is a parallelogram. If the area of square ABIH is 20, what is the area of parallelogram BJFI?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 300 260" width="300" height="260" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><polygon points="40,180 200,60 240,60 80,180" fill="#e5edf7" stroke="none"/><g stroke="#1f2937" fill="none" stroke-width="2"><rect x="40" y="20" width="200" height="200"/><rect x="40" y="180" width="40" height="40"/><rect x="200" y="20" width="40" height="40"/><polygon points="40,180 200,60 240,60 80,180"/></g><g font-family="Georgia, serif" font-size="14" fill="#1f2937"><text x="26" y="234">A</text><text x="24" y="186">B</text><text x="26" y="16">C</text><text x="192" y="14">D</text><text x="244" y="16">E</text><text x="246" y="64">F</text><text x="244" y="234">G</text><text x="74" y="236">H</text><text x="87" y="197">I</text><text x="185" y="48">J</text></g></svg>
questions.explanation: Let each small square have side s, so its area is s^2 = 20. Since square ACEG has 25 times that area, its side is 5s. Put A at the origin with AG along one axis and AC along the other. Then B is s from A along AC and I is the far corner of the small square, so segment BI is horizontal with length s and sits s from side AG. The far small square at E puts J and F at a height of 5s - s = 4s, with JF horizontal of length s. So BJFI has base BI = s and its opposite side JF parallel to it at a height of 4s - s = 3s. Its area is base times height = s(3s) = 3s^2 = 3(20) = 60.
questions.trap: Students take the parallelogram's height to be the full 4s that separates the two small squares' far edges and answer 80, or they slide the slanted side BJ into the area formula and use it as a height. The height of a parallelogram is the perpendicular distance between the two parallel sides BI and JF, which is 3s, not 4s and not the slant.
questions.ets_note: Stem narrates the figure and restates conditions redundantly; wordy for ETS.

ets_rescore.prev_note: Stem is long and over-specified (states equal areas, parallelogram, ratio).

questions.question:
The distance from the centre of tree P to the centre of tree Q is 30 feet, and the distance from the centre of tree P to the centre of tree R is 18 feet. The centres of the three trees are not in a straight line. Which of the following could be the distance, in feet, from the centre of tree Q to the centre of tree R?

Indicate all such values.
questions.explanation: The three centres form a triangle, so QR must be greater than the difference of the other two sides and less than their sum: 30 - 18 = 12 and 30 + 18 = 48, giving 12 < QR < 48. Of the choices, 20, 36 and 45 lie strictly inside. 10 is below the range, and 12 and 48 are the excluded endpoints.
questions.trap: Students include 12 or 48, the two boundary values. Each of those would place the three centres on a single line, which the problem explicitly rules out, so both bounds are open.
questions.ets_note: Near-identical template to SEC-PG-023 (two distances, non-collinear, select-all triangle inequality).

questions.question:
Square WXYZ and parallelogram WPQZ lie in the same plane and share the side WZ. Also, WP = WX, points P and X lie on the same side of line WZ, and P is not the same point as X. Which of the following must be true?

Indicate all such statements.
options: A. The area of WXYZ is greater than the area of WPQZ
B. The perimeter of WXYZ is equal to the perimeter of WPQZ
D. The area of WPQZ is greater than half the area of WXYZ
E. The area of WXYZ is more than twice the area of WPQZ
questions.explanation: Let the shared side WZ have length a. The square has all four sides equal to a. Since WP = WX = a, the parallelogram has WP = a as well, and in a parallelogram opposite sides are equal, so PQ = WZ = a and ZQ = WP = a. That settles two statements at once: PQ = a = XY, so C is true, and both figures have perimeter 4a, so B is true. For areas, both figures sit on base WZ = a. The square's height is the full a, because WX is perpendicular to WZ. The parallelogram's height is a times the sine of angle PWZ. Because P and X lie on the same side of line WZ with WP = WX = a, both P and X sit on the same semicircle of radius a centred at W, so P not equal to X forces angle PWZ to differ from angle XWZ = 90 degrees. The sine is then strictly less than 1 and the parallelogram's area is strictly less than a^2. So A is true. But nothing pins down how far the parallelogram leans: the angle could be near 90 degrees, making its area almost a^2, or very small, making its area nearly zero. So D and E can each fail, and the parallelogram's diagonal WQ likewise varies with the lean while WY is fixed at a*sqrt(2), so F can fail.
questions.trap: Students reject B, assuming a leaning shape must have a different perimeter from the square. Tilting the square into a rhombus keeps every side at length a, so the perimeter is untouched; it is the area, which depends on the height, that shrinks.
